item.title: Photos: ADC supporters rally in large numbers for campaign flag-off in Sokoto
item.description: By Musa Ubandawaki, Sokoto The slogan “Tinubu Must Go” reverberated across the venue of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential campaign flag-off along Illorin Road in Sokoto metropolis on Wednesday, as supporters of the opposition party expressed their opposition to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration ahead of the 2027 general elections. The slogan, which became a recurring chant among the crowd, reflected the determination of ADC supporters to mobilise Nigerians for political change and challenge the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) at the polls. The chant gained momentum as supporters, many of whom had travelled from different parts of Sokoto State, expressed solidarity with the ADC and its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar. The rally also provided an opportunity for supporters to express dissatisfaction with the Tinubu administration, particularly over the economic challenges confronting Nigerians and persistent security concerns affecting communities across the country. The development highlighted the ADC’s efforts to strengthen its support base in Sokoto State and mobilise grassroots support ahead of the 2027 general elections. As the party intensifies its nationwide mobilisation, the rally offered a platform for opposition supporters to communicate their grievances and demand political change. However, as of the time of filing this report, the ADC presidential campaign train was yet to arrive at the venue from the Sultan Abubakar III International Airport, Sokoto, reportedly due to the large crowd along the route. The post Photos: ADC supporters rally in large numbers for campaign flag-off in Sokoto appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: 2027: No coalition needed in Ondo, APC elders declare
item.description: Target one million votes for Tinubu, 80% turnout By Dayo Johnson, Akure The PBAT Mandate Elders Forum (PMF), Ondo State chapter, has declared that there is no need for a coalition arrangement in the state ahead of the 2027 general elections, insisting that the All Progressives Congress (APC) is strong enough to win all elective positions. The Forum also set a target of at least one million votes for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election, alongside an 80 per cent voter turnout in the state. The position was made known at a meeting of the Forum in Akure, the state capital, where its chairman, Hon. Demola Ijabiyi, said the APC’s dominance in the state made any arrangement requiring it to surrender candidates or constituencies unnecessary. Ijabiyi said the Forum recognised the importance of cooperation among political parties with shared political objectives but maintained that such arrangements must reflect the political realities of individual states. “In Ondo State, the APC is the dominant political party, controlling government at both the state and local government levels,” he said. He said the Forum welcomed support from other political parties for Tinubu’s re-election but would not accept any arrangement that required APC candidates to step down. “Support for the President need not depend on displacing APC candidates. We have confidence in our candidates and their prospects of victory,” he said. According to him, coalition arrangements are more appropriate in states where political parties have limited electoral strength and need to combine forces to overcome their weaknesses. He explained that parties could support stronger candidates in constituencies where they lacked sufficient electoral strength in exchange for reciprocal support elsewhere. “But we don’t have that kind of circumstance in Ondo State. There is no constituency that we cannot win. There is no constituency that we do not want to contest. We are going to win all. That is the bottom line,” he said. The Forum chairman also cited the declining political strength of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), which he described as the major opposition party in the state in the past, as another reason the APC should not surrender its electoral interests. On mobilisation, Ijabiyi said the Forum was working towards extending its structures to every ward and polling unit to mobilise voters and secure victory for Tinubu and all APC candidates. He said Ondo State’s more than two million registered voters ahead of the 2027 governorship election presented a significant electoral opportunity, adding that the challenge was to translate the figure into actual voter participation. “We have therefore set a voter turnout target of at least 80 per cent. The PMF will work towards this through sustained mobilisation and voter education. Alongside this, we must earn sufficient support to deliver at least one million votes for the President,” he said. Ijabiyi directed the Forum’s chapters to develop practical grassroots mobilisation plans, assign responsibilities and provide regular reports on their activities. The chairman also urged APC National and State Assembly candidates to intensify their campaigns, identify areas of weak mobilisation and work with local party leaders to strengthen support at the polling-unit level. He said candidates should engage voters directly, explain their legislative priorities and demonstrate how their election would advance the interests of their constituencies. Ijabiyi further urged the candidates to promote Tinubu’s re-election and support the campaigns of other APC candidates, stressing that victory would depend on effective coordination among party structures and support groups. The Forum reaffirmed its commitment to Tinubu’s re-election and the victory of all APC candidates in the 2027 elections. It also pledged to collaborate with the party leadership, candidates, the Campaign Council and other support groups to mobilise support for the President ahead of his planned reception in the state on November 11. item.title: Trump seeks to shift blame but has 'nowhere to hide' after midterms defeat
item.description: Donald Trump has sought to shift the blame for the Republicans' defeat at the midterms by claiming that if he had been on the ballot the party would have won. But the "blue wave" that saw Democrats win control of Congress can be traced directly back to Trump's decisions, says France 24's Washington correspondent Fraser Jackson.

item.title: US Midterm Voters Deliver Brutal Verdict On Trump
item.description: Donald Trump faced a radically transformed and hostile political landscape on Wednesday after US voters handed control of Congress to the Democrats in a stunning rebuke to his presidency. The result was a personal humiliation for the 80-year-old Trump as a Democratic wave swept into his Republican heartland, boosted by anger at soaring energy costs and his costly, dragging war with Iran. The Democratic capture of both the Senate and the House of Representatives signals an end to Trump’s stranglehold on US politics and gives Democrats the power to block legislation, launch investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his appointments. The results reflected deep frustration over the cost of living, tariffs and Trump’s war with Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president. “This is so incredibly exciting. We can get our country back,” Kathy Jackoway said in Texas, celebrating a win by Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Trump struck a conciliatory tone despite his history of rejecting election defeats, telling The New York Times he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results. “I think the Democrats did a good job,” the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. “They fought hard.” Combo image of Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (r) and President of the U.S Donald Trump (l) But he sought to distance himself from his party’s poor showing, adding: “I don’t view it as a hit on me.” He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the result but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration. Republican Heartland Democrats flipped seats that had long been held by Republicans, scoring breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine. In Maine, former logger Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins. In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932. Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008. In Texas, Democrats won not only a Senate seat but also the governor’s race, ending decades of Republican rule. Democrats protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress. El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curveball when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers. In the House, Democrats made gains in Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Arizona, North Carolina, Wisconsin and New Jersey, including districts Trump had carried comfortably in 2024. Democrats also won Georgia’s governorship, electing former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman gove

item.content:encoded: Donald Trump faced a radically transformed and hostile political landscape on Wednesday after US voters handed control of Congress to the Democrats in a stunning rebuke to his presidency. The result was a personal humiliation for the 80-year-old Trump as a Democratic wave swept into his Republican heartland, boosted by anger at soaring energy costs and his costly, dragging war with Iran. The Democratic capture of both the Senate and the House of Representatives signals an end to Trump’s stranglehold on US politics and gives Democrats the power to block legislation, launch investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his appointments. The results reflected deep frustration over the cost of living, tariffs and Trump’s war with Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president. “This is so incredibly exciting. We can get our country back,” Kathy Jackoway said in Texas, celebrating a win by Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. Trump struck a conciliatory tone despite his history of rejecting election defeats, telling The New York Times he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results. “I think the Democrats did a good job,” the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. “They fought hard.” Combo image of Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (r) and President of the U.S Donald Trump (l) But he sought to distance himself from his party’s poor showing, adding: “I don’t view it as a hit on me.” He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the result but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration. Republican Heartland Democrats flipped seats that had long been held by Republicans, scoring breakthroughs in South Carolina, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas and Maine. In Maine, former logger Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Senator Susan Collins. In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932. Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008. In Texas, Democrats won not only a Senate seat but also the governor’s race, ending decades of Republican rule. Democrats protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress. El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curveball when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers. In the House, Democrats made gains in Pennsylvania, Kentucky, Arizona, North Carolina, Wisconsin and New Jersey, including districts Trump had carried comfortably in 2024. Democrats also won Georgia’s governorship, electing former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms as the first Black woman governor in US history. Republicans had some consolation in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds became the state’s first Black governor and Ashley Moody retained a Senate seat. But the night was “a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies,” George Washington University professor Todd Belt told AFP. Trump On Defensive House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run.” Jeffries could become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January. Trump insisted on social media that Republicans would have won “IN A LANDSLIDE” if he had been running, though he had repeatedly urged supporters throughout the campaign to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” He also repeated his threat to use the presidential veto on Democrat-passed bills, posting a picture on social media of a red baseball cap reading just: “VETO.” On the international front, Russia said it hoped Trump will continue his “peacemaking efforts” and China said it would “continue working” with the United States. Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he did not expect the election results to bring about a shift in US policy. AFP The post US Midterm Voters Deliver Brutal Verdict On Trump appeared first on Channels Television .

item.title: Police warn politicians against destroying campaign materials
item.description: …IGP orders commissioners to arrest, prosecute offenders By Kingsley Omonobi The Nigeria Police Force has warned politicians, political thugs and other individuals against the destruction or defacement of campaign posters, banners and billboards belonging to candidates and political parties ahead of the 2027 general elections. The Force said offenders would be arrested and prosecuted, warning that political differences or loyalty to a particular party did not give anyone the right to destroy another candidate’s campaign materials. Force Public Relations Officer, CSP Aniete Iniedu, disclosed this in a statement on Wednesday, saying the police had observed with concern growing incidents of deliberate tearing, defacement and destruction of campaign materials across the country. The statement read: “The Nigeria Police Force strongly condemns this act of political intolerance and warns political thugs, hoodlums and other mischief-makers involved to desist immediately. “For the avoidance of doubt, destroying, defacing or unlawfully removing another candidate’s campaign posters and billboards may constitute malicious damage, which is a criminal offence under applicable criminal laws, including Section 451 of the Criminal Code Act and Section 326 of the Penal Code Law, which defines the offence of mischief. “Political differences or loyalty to a particular party do not give anyone the right to destroy another candidate’s property or infringe on their right to campaign freely. “The Force reiterates that all political parties and candidates, irrespective of their affiliation or status, are entitled to equal protection under the law. “No individual or group has the right to determine whose campaign materials should be displayed or destroyed.” The police said the Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu, had directed commissioners of police in the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory to take proactive measures to prevent such incidents. He also directed them to investigate reported cases and ensure that anyone found culpable was arrested and prosecuted in accordance with the law. The statement added that political sponsors and individuals who recruited, encouraged or facilitated the destruction of campaign materials would also be held accountable where evidence established their involvement. The Force urged political parties, candidates and their supporters to conduct their campaigns peacefully and respect the rights of others. It warned that political intolerance, intimidation and criminal conduct must not be allowed to undermine the democratic process. “The Nigeria Police Force will not allow political thugs and troublemakers to turn the nation’s political environment into a theatre of lawlessness. Those who choose to break the law will face the full consequences of their actions. “Be warned. Respect the law. Let democracy thrive,” the statement added. The post Police warn politicians against destroying campaign materials appeared first

item.title: Australia’s social media ban faces high court challenge
item.description: Australian teenagers are still using social media apps Shutterstock/Tada Images Almost one year on from the start of Australia’s landmark social media ban, it is clear that the law has failed to stop most children from accessing the platforms. Meanwhile, teenagers are hoping to overturn the policy through a challenge at the nation’s highest court. “I’m bringing the High Court case because young Australians have a right to be in the digital town square,” says Noah Jones, a primary witness opposing the ban in the case, which started hearings on 3 November. “This is the world of technology and I’m entitled to see it all and not be shut out.” Read more The truth about social media and screen time’s impact on young people Jones was 15 when the ban came into effect , prohibiting under-16s from accessing social media sites, including Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat and TikTok. He was a plaintiff in the case, but withdrew due to the risk of costs being awarded against his family. Advertisement Now, the constitutional challenge is being led by advocacy group the Digital Freedom Project, alongside Reddit, which – like other social media behemoths – fears that Australia’s social media ban will be replicated elsewhere around the world. The primary argument before the court this week has been that the ban limits the freedom of political communication for under-16s. In spite of this challenge and widespread concerns about implementing and enforcing a social media ban for children, numerous nations, including the UK , Indonesia, Malaysia, Brazil and a number of EU members, say they, too, will follow suit. Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter From the moment the policy was announced, many experts warned that it would be unworkable and could have negative outcomes , and that the real target of any policy should be the platforms, their algorithms and what they allow online. The biggest failure of the policy highlighted by researchers is that most children have been able to keep their profiles. One study by Courtney Barnes at the University of Newcastle in Australia and her colleagues, who surveyed more than 400 under-16s prior to the ban and then again three months after it, found that 85 per cent were still using prohibited platforms. Such research and similar findings from Australia’s eSafety commissioner forced the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, to announce in June a doubling of the fines for social media companies from AUS$49.5 million to AUS$99 million ($35 million to $69 million) if breaches were identified. He also introduced a raft of new powers for the eSafety commissioner to compel companies to provide information about what they were doing to get kids off their sites. At that time, Albanese said countries around the world were following Australia’s lead on social media reform, but that social media companies weren’t doing enough to exclude children. item.dc:creator: James Woodford
item.content:encoded: Australian teenagers are still using social media apps Shutterstock/Tada Images Almost one year on from the start of Australia’s landmark social media ban, it is clear that the law has failed to stop most children from accessing the platforms. Meanwhile, teenagers are hoping to overturn the policy through a challenge at the nation’s highest court. “I’m bringing the High Court case because young Australians have a right to be in the digital town square,” says Noah Jones, a primary witness opposing the ban in the case, which started hearings on 3 November. “This is the world of technology and I’m entitled to see it all and not be shut out.” Read more The truth about social media and screen time’s impact on young people Jones was 15 when the ban came into effect , prohibiting under-16s from accessing social media sites, including Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat and TikTok. He was a plaintiff in the case, but withdrew due to the risk of costs being awarded against his family. Advertisement Now, the constitutional challenge is being led by advocacy group the Digital Freedom Project, alongside Reddit, which – like other social media behemoths – fears that Australia’s social media ban will be replicated elsewhere around the world. The primary argument before the court this week has been that the ban limits the freedom of political communication for under-16s. In spite of this challenge and widespread concerns about implementing and enforcing a social media ban for children, numerous nations, including the UK , Indonesia, Malaysia, Brazil and a number of EU members, say they, too, will follow suit. Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter From the moment the policy was announced, many experts warned that it would be unworkable and could have negative outcomes , and that the real target of any policy should be the platforms, their algorithms and what they allow online. The biggest failure of the policy highlighted by researchers is that most children have been able to keep their profiles. One study by Courtney Barnes at the University of Newcastle in Australia and her colleagues, who surveyed more than 400 under-16s prior to the ban and then again three months after it, found that 85 per cent were still using prohibited platforms. Such research and similar findings from Australia’s eSafety commissioner forced the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, to announce in June a doubling of the fines for social media companies from AUS$49.5 million to AUS$99 million ($35 million to $69 million) if breaches were identified. He also introduced a raft of new powers for the eSafety commissioner to compel companies to provide information about what they were doing to get kids off their sites. At that time, Albanese said countries around the world were following Australia’s lead on social media reform, but that social media companies weren’t doing enough to exclude children. Yet, nearly half a year later, and in spite of widespread evidence that the laws have had little effect on teens’ social media use, not a single fine has so far been issued. “Some kids hid accounts and devices from parents at first, but when accounts shut down, we all just made a new one or had someone older do the face scan,” says Jones. “Kids just laughed and kept using socials. Most kids I know have more social media accounts than last year because new platforms popped up and we tried them out.” Read more How AI poisoning is fighting bots that hoover data without permission Iain Corby at the Age Verification Providers Association in London says up to 80 per cent of children have kept their accounts, with half saying they were never challenged and over a third retaining access “thanks to the false ages they originally used to create the account”. “Australia has been a missed opportunity for those who hoped it would provide evidence on the benefits and drawbacks of age restrictions for social media, because the platforms did not implement the law in good faith,” says Corby. He says the UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has been much clearer about the requirement for highly effective age assurance when the UK brings in its restrictions next spring, and that ministers are “alive to the need for robust legislation that pre-empts loopholes”. “The social media platforms may think they have muddied the waters and avoided a successful precedent being set by Australia, but it is clear that lessons are also being learned by observers.” Susan McLean at CyberSafety Solutions, an Australian consultancy, says it is sad that teens around the world can access Instagram teen accounts with inbuilt safety settings, limited content and algorithmic controls, yet Australian children cannot because of the ban. She says this is pushing them to far less safe platforms. “I would never have found primary kids even knowing what Reddit was before the ban, but now it’s mainstream for kids as their vetting is easily bypassed,” says McLean. Read more Social media is dead – here’s what comes next Catherine Page Jeffery at the University of Sydney says her children have been able to retain their social media accounts and a “tentative conclusion” can be drawn that not that much has changed for Australian teens. She says there is no point doubling the penalty for social media firm breaches if the government isn’t going to enforce the law. “What does enforcement look like? Are we going to see that? Are we going to see these platforms being taken to court?” Jeffery asks. Lisa Given at RMIT University in Melbourne says governments around the world have been captivated by the headlines rather than the data. Instead of bans, efforts should instead be on online safety and digital duty of care, she says. It is impossible to keep children from interacting online and the focus of governments should be on making platforms safe, says Given. “My main message is that this isn’t the solution,” she says. “I think other countries really need to actually look at the data.” Noah Jones, the young witness in the High Court case, says the arguments made by the government’s lawyers in court this week left him dismayed. “I don’t matter as an Australian when they say I’m not an elector and they do not seem to know the shorthand of how people communicate today,” he says. “I resent when statements are made that I should form a local club to exchange ideas or drop pamphlets – that sounds like my mum’s childhood before the internet.”

item.title: A third of babies with peanut allergy grow out of it by 1 year old
item.description: Peanut allergies are common, but aren’t always lifelong Shutterstock/Aleksandr Grechanyuk More than a third of babies who were previously diagnosed with peanut allergies safely tolerated them during subsequent testing. This suggests that a surprisingly high proportion of infants’ peanut allergies last less than one year, allowing them to be freed from a lifetime of food restriction and worry. “Being able to identify those children early allows them to avoid an unnecessary allergy label and the burden of avoiding peanut,” says Tim Brettig at Murdoch Children’s Research Institute in Melbourne. Read more The new drugs preventing allergic reactions to peanuts and other foods Since 2024, Australia has offered free treatment to all babies diagnosed with peanut allergy under the age of 12 months. The treatment, overseen by 10 public children’s hospitals across the country, involves feeding small but gradually increasing doses of peanut flour to allergic infants over two years to try to desensitise them, a strategy known as oral immunotherapy. Advertisement Before beginning the programme, babies are required to undergo an “oral food challenge” to confirm their allergy and assess its severity. It involves feeding them gradually escalating doses of peanut flour on a single day under medical supervision to see how much they can tolerate. The total given is 2500 milligrams, equivalent to two teaspoons of peanut butter. This is “above the threshold where we’d expect all children of this age to react if they have an allergy”, says Brettig, the medical lead of the programme. However, of the first 778 babies with previously diagnosed peanut allergy who undertook the oral food challenge, 35 per cent did not react to any dose of the peanut flour. This was despite the fact they had previously developed rashes, swelling, hives or other signs of allergic reactions after consuming peanut-containing foods, and had skin prick or blood test results consistent with a peanut allergy. “This was a surprising result for us – we expected a small proportion might pass the food challenge, but not 35 per cent,” says Brettig. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The parents of these babies were given the good news that their child was no longer considered to have a peanut allergy and didn’t need to begin the oral immunotherapy programme. They were also assured that they could safely reintroduce peanut into their child’s diet at home. The average time between the initial diagnosis of the peanut allergy and the oral food challenge was six months. It is unclear why a third of the infants stopped having reactions to peanut in this short window. “It might be that they had a transient allergy, where the immune system has an aberrant response to a food initially, but it doesn’t continue to occur,” says Brettig. item.dc:creator: Alice Klein
item.content:encoded: Peanut allergies are common, but aren’t always lifelong Shutterstock/Aleksandr Grechanyuk More than a third of babies who were previously diagnosed with peanut allergies safely tolerated them during subsequent testing. This suggests that a surprisingly high proportion of infants’ peanut allergies last less than one year, allowing them to be freed from a lifetime of food restriction and worry. “Being able to identify those children early allows them to avoid an unnecessary allergy label and the burden of avoiding peanut,” says Tim Brettig at Murdoch Children’s Research Institute in Melbourne. Read more The new drugs preventing allergic reactions to peanuts and other foods Since 2024, Australia has offered free treatment to all babies diagnosed with peanut allergy under the age of 12 months. The treatment, overseen by 10 public children’s hospitals across the country, involves feeding small but gradually increasing doses of peanut flour to allergic infants over two years to try to desensitise them, a strategy known as oral immunotherapy. Advertisement Before beginning the programme, babies are required to undergo an “oral food challenge” to confirm their allergy and assess its severity. It involves feeding them gradually escalating doses of peanut flour on a single day under medical supervision to see how much they can tolerate. The total given is 2500 milligrams, equivalent to two teaspoons of peanut butter. This is “above the threshold where we’d expect all children of this age to react if they have an allergy”, says Brettig, the medical lead of the programme. However, of the first 778 babies with previously diagnosed peanut allergy who undertook the oral food challenge, 35 per cent did not react to any dose of the peanut flour. This was despite the fact they had previously developed rashes, swelling, hives or other signs of allergic reactions after consuming peanut-containing foods, and had skin prick or blood test results consistent with a peanut allergy. “This was a surprising result for us – we expected a small proportion might pass the food challenge, but not 35 per cent,” says Brettig. Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter The parents of these babies were given the good news that their child was no longer considered to have a peanut allergy and didn’t need to begin the oral immunotherapy programme. They were also assured that they could safely reintroduce peanut into their child’s diet at home. The average time between the initial diagnosis of the peanut allergy and the oral food challenge was six months. It is unclear why a third of the infants stopped having reactions to peanut in this short window. “It might be that they had a transient allergy, where the immune system has an aberrant response to a food initially, but it doesn’t continue to occur,” says Brettig. Previous research has found that roughly a third of children with peanut allergies naturally grow out of them by age 6 , but this is the first time a high proportion of peanut allergies have been found to resolve on their own in infants. First week of life seems crucial for future allergy and eczema risk The mainstream view is that there are no particularly critical phases in the development of the immune system, but a study of hundreds of infants suggests otherwise The finding will “make a huge difference” to the children whose allergy labels were removed, says Brettig, because they won’t have to spend their lives being burdened by restricted food choices, anxiety about accidental exposure to peanut and the need to carry emergency medication. It may also prevent them from developing a true peanut allergy down the track, since peanut avoidance in early life is known to increase the risk of allergies later on , he says. The results also have wider implications for how peanut allergy is diagnosed and managed, says John Ziegler at the University of New South Wales, Sydney. Peanut allergy is commonly diagnosed based on clinical history and the results of skin prick or blood tests, usually without an oral food challenge. Routinely conducting oral food challenges would identify those who don’t need require treatment, and thus be cost-effective, says Ziegler. “The study confirms the importance of confirmation of the diagnosis of peanut allergy before embarking on oral immunotherapy,” he says. Due to the risk of severe reactions like anaphylaxis, such allergy treatments should only be conducted under medical supervision. Journal Reference: The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology: In Practice DOI: 10.1016/j.jaip.2026.08.044

item.title: ‘Discontent and distrust’: annual social cohesion checkup shows exactly what’s making Australia angry
item.description: Cost of living and AI outrank climate change and war as top concerns for future, but support for multiculturalism remains strong Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The vast majority of Australians support immigration and multiculturalism despite more feeling poorer – and increasingly pessimistic and distrustful of government, the annual Scanlon report on social cohesion has revealed. People are more worried about artificial intelligence than climate change or going to war, but a global economic downturn and cost-of-living pressures are Australians’ key concerns. item.title: Faraway’s Unprecedented 16-Year Development Has Resulted in an Instant Classic
item.description: Faraway is the latest game from Steph Thirion, the solo developer behind 2009’s critically acclaimed iOS puzzler Eliss . (It’s published by Annapurna Interactive , the company arguably best-known for publishing offbeat games for wider audiences.) At a distance, Faraway looks like a small project: a high-score chasing arcade game about shooting stars. In reality, it’s a 16-year passion project that has finally come to fruition. Even in its one-button simplicity, Faraway feels like the kind of small-scale masterwork that so often gets overlooked in an industry that increasingly values Hollywood production over expressive gameplay.

item.title: Does opting out of TV tracking work?
item.description: TVs use automatic content recognition to gather viewing information about us, and opting out doesn’t always stop it. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge The fact our TVs are gathering our information isn't new, but what and how they're tracking - and if we can stop it - is hard to figure out. Researchers at Northeastern University monitored 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers to test whether opting out of automatic content recognition (ACR) actually works . While opting out was effective for most TVs - including LG, Amazon Fire TV, a Sony Bravia running Google TV, and those with Vidaa OS (which can be found on TVs from Hisense, Toshiba, and smaller brands like the Supersonic used in the study) - Samsung and Roku kept sending some data. And Walmart's Vizio TV continued on as if the opt-out hadn't eve … Read the full story at The Verge.

While opting out was effective for most TVs - including LG, Amazon Fire TV, a Sony Bravia running Google TV, and those with Vidaa OS (which can be found on TVs from Hisense, Toshiba, and smaller brands like the Supersonic used in the study) - Samsung and Roku kept sending some data. And Walmart's Vizio TV continued on as if the opt-out hadn't eve … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Hannah Fry: How to win The Traitors with maths (step one, don’t get made a traitor)
item.description: Hannah Fry in The Celebrity Traitors BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry In the late 1980s, in Soviet-era Russia, a young psychologist called Dmitry Davydov came up with a game about power and information. He called it Mafia and originally intended it as a teaching device, a way to demonstrate how a small, informed minority could manipulate the dynamics of a much larger, uninformed group and wield outsized power over those who were left floundering in uncertainty and paranoia. Almost 40 years later, that game has evolved into The Traitors – a TV show that is such a massive cultural phenomenon in the UK that the opening episode of this year’s celebrity edition drew more viewers to BBC One than watched England’s World Cup semi-final against Argentina. And recently I found myself in the middle of it. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Professor Hannah Fry’s column Sign up to newsletter In case you’ve been living under a rock, or just happen to have better things to do with your life than watch reality television (in which case, lucky you), the premise is simple. A small number of players, the traitors, secretly know who is on their side and get to “murder” someone each night. The remaining players, the faithful, are tasked with working out who the traitors are, voting to banish one suspect each evening. Inevitably, they spend most of their time rounding on innocent people and making them disintegrate. Which I strongly suspect might be at least half of what makes the whole thing so damn entertaining. Here’s the thing. When I got the call asking if I wanted to be on the show, of course I jumped at the chance. A game of incomplete information? That’s a mathematician’s dream, I thought. What a fun, stress-free way to try out some of my theories. On reflection, past me was an idiot. But we’ll come to that. Read more The surprising science that reveals what it takes to win The Traitors The challenge, as I saw it, was to find a way to cut through the uncertainty. All I had to do was monitor the evidence as the game unfolded, use the patterns in people’s behaviour to identify the traitors and then just persuade everyone else to vote them out. Bish bash bosh, victory. I started by combing through every previous series of the UK show, turning the joyful, chaotic mess of the series into a clean, delicious spreadsheet, determined to use all the statistical tricks I had at my disposal. item.dc:creator: Hannah Fry
item.content:encoded: Hannah Fry in The Celebrity Traitors BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry In the late 1980s, in Soviet-era Russia, a young psychologist called Dmitry Davydov came up with a game about power and information. He called it Mafia and originally intended it as a teaching device, a way to demonstrate how a small, informed minority could manipulate the dynamics of a much larger, uninformed group and wield outsized power over those who were left floundering in uncertainty and paranoia. Almost 40 years later, that game has evolved into The Traitors – a TV show that is such a massive cultural phenomenon in the UK that the opening episode of this year’s celebrity edition drew more viewers to BBC One than watched England’s World Cup semi-final against Argentina. And recently I found myself in the middle of it. Advertisement Free newsletter Sign up to Professor Hannah Fry’s column Sign up to newsletter In case you’ve been living under a rock, or just happen to have better things to do with your life than watch reality television (in which case, lucky you), the premise is simple. A small number of players, the traitors, secretly know who is on their side and get to “murder” someone each night. The remaining players, the faithful, are tasked with working out who the traitors are, voting to banish one suspect each evening. Inevitably, they spend most of their time rounding on innocent people and making them disintegrate. Which I strongly suspect might be at least half of what makes the whole thing so damn entertaining. Here’s the thing. When I got the call asking if I wanted to be on the show, of course I jumped at the chance. A game of incomplete information? That’s a mathematician’s dream, I thought. What a fun, stress-free way to try out some of my theories. On reflection, past me was an idiot. But we’ll come to that. Read more The surprising science that reveals what it takes to win The Traitors The challenge, as I saw it, was to find a way to cut through the uncertainty. All I had to do was monitor the evidence as the game unfolded, use the patterns in people’s behaviour to identify the traitors and then just persuade everyone else to vote them out. Bish bash bosh, victory. I started by combing through every previous series of the UK show, turning the joyful, chaotic mess of the series into a clean, delicious spreadsheet, determined to use all the statistical tricks I had at my disposal. Who voted for whom? Who travelled in cars together? Were there subtle statistical differences in the way traitors and faithful behaved that might give the game away? It turned out there were. For example, I discovered that traitors often make what I came to think of as “burn votes”. They don’t necessarily want to send down an innocent person, nor do they want to persuade others into joining a stampede, drawing attention to themselves in the process. So, instead, they throw their vote away on someone nobody else is voting for. They will also vote to banish their fellow traitors, but only when the writing is already on the wall. Someone who suddenly joins the vote against a traitor on the night they are finally banished, having never voted for them before, was a signal worth keeping an eye on. There were clues pointing in the other direction, too: failing to vote for a traitor on the night they are banished turned out to be a good signal that someone is faithful. And then there was a particularly ingenious observation made by viewers online: the producers often send the players who were shortlisted for murder into breakfast last. Occasionally, they throw one traitor into that group to keep everyone guessing, but never two. Which means that if someone arrived late to breakfast alongside a player who was subsequently revealed to be a traitor, that was a potentially useful clue that they were faithful. From left: Joanne McNally, Maya Jama, Julie Hesmondhalgh and Hannah Fry at breakfast in The Celebrity Traitors BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan Cherry As far as I could tell, there were no surefire ways to identify someone as a traitor (although Richard E. Grant would later do a spectacular job of proving me wrong). The faithful are so gloriously unpredictable (ahem. Joanne McNally) that anything suspicious could almost as easily have been done by a perfectly innocent player. But even so, buried in the noise, there were some small signals that could accumulate over time. Fortunately, there is a neat mathematical way to combine lots of weak evidence together – and it just so happens to have been used by Alan Turing to help crack the enigma code in the second world war. So, inspired by Turing, with a little help from our mutual, close personal friend Thomas Bayes, I set about building a Bayesian model that I could bring with me into the castle. It’s actually pretty simple: a points system that lets you update the odds of someone being a traitor as you go. The scores came from what had happened in previous series, and are almost entirely based on people’s voting patterns. +0.47 for a burn vote. -0.83 if you fail to vote for a traitor on the night they go down. For the nerdier among you, the units I was using are nats – a measure of how strongly the accumulated evidence favours one hypothesis over another – but you can just think of them as traitor points. I was as confident as I could be that, at the very least, the famous words of statistician George E. P. Box would prove true: “All models are wrong, but some are useful.” Read more Hannah Fry: How OpenAI has caused an existential crisis in mathematics Unfortunately, there was one rather significant problem with my plan. Within about 15 minutes of arriving in the castle, they made me a traitor. (Technically I could have refused, but it happened in such a way that it would have meant my immediate downfall.) I went back to my room and sobbed into my spreadsheets. Still, I’m not about to let the small matter of being made a traitor (and catastrophically failing to be deceitful on national television ) get in the way of a good mathematical experiment. So, now that the final has aired and I know the way that the votes fell, I can finally run the numbers to see how the model would have played out in real time. And I’m delighted to say that the maths worked. Brilliantly, in fact. At every single round table, the maths has a traitor as top, or joint top. Not every innocent player escaped suspicion, and the model certainly wasn’t infallible. But there really are signals buried in that noise, and you really can use mathematics to detect them. (And yes, the irony that literally being buried is what got me into this mess is not lost on me). The trouble is, a mathematical model has one enormous advantage over a contestant on The Traitors . It doesn’t have to convince anyone to trust it. It doesn’t have to worry about being murdered or defend itself against accusations over breakfast, while trying to remember what normal facial expressions look like. And so even if I’d been a faithful, I suspect there was never any realistic chance of putting the mathematics to use within the game itself. Because, as Mafia was designed to demonstrate, the real power in a game like this isn’t just knowing the truth, it’s being able to shape what everyone else believes. And so, George, it turns out some models are right. It’s just that, sometimes, that’s the least of your problems. Hannah Fry: I lost my dad to Alzheimer’s. New research into its origins is amazing My lovely father died of Alzheimer’s last year, and since then, I’ve been digging into the disease to try to understand what happened to him. I was astonished to discover that scientists think it may start in the nose, says New Scientist’s new columnist, Professor Hannah Fry

item.title: State Police Bill to reach Tinubu for assent today — Reps
item.description: By Gift Chapi Odekina, Abuja ABUJA — The State Police Bill, seeking to decentralise policing responsibilities between the Federal and state governments, will be transmitted to President Bola Tinubu on Wednesday for assent. The Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, disclosed this while presiding over plenary, following the approval of the proposed constitutional amendment by 29 of the 36 State Houses of Assembly. Kalu expressed excitement over the endorsement of the proposed police reform by more than two-thirds of the state legislatures, describing the development as a major step towards the establishment of state police in Nigeria. “The State Police Bill has received the backing of 29 State Assemblies. Later today, the Clerk to the National Assembly will transmit it to the President for assent,” he said. The approval by the state assemblies marks a significant milestone in efforts to amend the Constitution to allow states to establish and manage their own police forces alongside the Nigeria Police Force. The proposed reform is aimed at addressing concerns over Nigeria’s centralised policing structure, which critics argue limits the capacity of security agencies to respond effectively to local security challenges. Under the proposed arrangement, state governments would have greater responsibility for policing within their jurisdictions, while the Federal Government would retain its own police structure. The reform is expected to allow states to develop policing strategies tailored to their security needs, with the aim of strengthening intelligence gathering, community-based security and responses to crime. The transmission of the bill to the President marks the next stage in the constitutional amendment process, following its passage by the National Assembly and approval by the required number of state legislatures. The proposed establishment of state police has remained a major issue in Nigeria’s security reform debate, with supporters advocating decentralised policing as a means of improving security management across the country. The post State Police Bill to reach Tinubu for assent today — Reps appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Fortnite's Latest Reward Is So Good, It's Creating a Black Market
item.description: Fortnite launched its treasure hunting season this Sunday, which includes a One Piece collaboration that was one of the most anticipated collaborations of all time. No one expected a new item to steal the show, overshadowing the One Piece skins players had been requesting for years. Fans have been obsessing over the Pirate Shop access token, a recently introduced item that makes the whole Item Shop free for a fortnight. Thankfully, they might be able to end their search earlier than expected, as Treasure Hours are scheduled to begin soon.

item.title: UNICEF commends Taraba over education reforms
item.description: … As state launches Learning Passport in 50 pilot schools By Femi Bolaji JALINGO — The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has commended the Taraba State Government for its education reforms, particularly the introduction of free and compulsory basic and secondary education, abolition of illegal school fees and distribution of free learning materials. The commendation was given by UNICEF Chief of Field Office, Bauchi, Dr Nuzhat Rafique, during the official launch of the Nigeria Learning Passport (NLP) in Jalingo. Rafique, who was represented by the Education Officer, UNICEF Bauchi Field Office, Raphael Aiyedipe, said the state’s education policies had contributed to an increase in school enrolment from approximately 760,000 to more than one million pupils since the inception of the current administration. She also applauded the government for promoting inclusive education for children with special needs, while strengthening teacher recruitment and professional development. According to her, the rollout of the digital learning platform was made possible through partnerships with Microsoft, the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), Airtel, IHS Towers and TECNO. She explained that the programme was designed to address connectivity barriers, reduce the number of out-of-school children and ensure continuity of learning, particularly in vulnerable communities. In his address, Governor Agbu Kefas reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to making education accessible to every child in the state, describing it as a cornerstone of sustainable development and national progress. Kefas, who was represented by the Head of Service, Dr Hamidu Kara, said the Nigeria Learning Passport represented a major step towards ensuring that no child was left behind in the state’s educational development. “The Nigerian Learning Passport represents a bold step forward in our commitment to ensure that no child is left behind in their educational journey, especially in these challenging times,” he said. He explained that the digital platform would provide flexible, accessible and inclusive learning opportunities, particularly for children affected by crises or disruptions to conventional schooling. The governor added that the initiative aligned with his administration’s free education agenda and urged stakeholders, teachers and students to embrace and promote the platform. Also speaking, the Commissioner for Secondary, Technical and Vocational Education, Dr Augustina Godwin, announced that the pilot phase of the programme would commence in 50 schools across the state. She assured that the government would expand the initiative to more schools to enable additional students to benefit from the digital learning platform. The post UNICEF commends Taraba over education reforms appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: US midterm candidates find something to agree on: Reining in datacenters
item.description: Datacenter restrictions found broad support among candidates for governor in this week's US midterm elections, with nearly all those examined by Data Center Watch backing bans, pauses, or tighter development rules. Data Center Watch, which tracks grassroots opposition to compute sheds across America, examined the public positions of 74 selected candidates across the 36 states that elected governors in the midterm elections on November 3. It found that 43 percent of those candidates supported a ban or moratorium on new projects, while another 51 percent backed further regulation or conditional development. Only about 5 percent had no stated public position. Support for bans or moratoriums crossed party lines, although it was more common among the Democratic candidates examined (60 percent) than Republicans (30 percent). Candidates from both major parties backed restrictions in eight states: Maryland, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon, Wisconsin, and Texas. Texas has experienced a boom in data campus development recently, thanks to its ample energy resources and light-touch regulations, although outgoing governor Greg Abbott ordered a pause earlier this year while audits of energy and water use were carried out. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Abbott in Tuesday's election and will take office in January. Those positions matter to developers because governors can shape state regulation, energy policy, and permitting, although approval powers vary by jurisdiction. However, temporary pauses and targeted construction restrictions do not necessarily amount to opposition to all datacenter development. AI-related campaign spending has also come under scrutiny. Guardrails Alliance, a labor-backed pressure group, described Leading the Future , a super PAC network opposing AI regulation, as "largely a non-factor" in the elections . It alleged the network avoided the most competitive races because "they know their money is politically toxic." Anti-datacenter sentiment has grown in the US in response to the facilities popping up in people's backyards, often without them having any say in the process. A Gallup survey earlier this year discovered that more than 70 percent of Americans would be against the construction of one in their neighborhood, while a Pew Research Center survey found that Americans increasingly believe datacenters are bad for the environment and blame them for rising household energy bills. Pew also found that advertisers spent almost $12 million on Facebook and Instagram political ads mentioning datacenters between July 27 and October 24. Among those running in October through the study's cutoff, 57 percent opposed datacenters and just three percent supported them. Common themes included corporate interests, energy use, environmental effects, and water consumption. ®

item.title: How military reduced nationwide attacks by 73 per cent in October as 217 terrorists neutralised
item.description: Troops of the Nigerian military have drastically reduced attacks across various theatres of operations in October 2026, Daily Trust reports. Checks showed that only 98 attacks were recorded during the month under review, representing a 73.3 per cent decline from the 367 attacks recorded in September. A breakdown of the October figures showed that Operation Enduring Peace recorded the highest number of attacks with 29 incidents, followed by Operation Hadin Kai with 27 and Operation Fansan Yamma with 24. Operation Whirl Stroke recorded 12 attacks, while Operation Udo Ka recorded four. Operations Delta Safe and Savannah Shield recorded one attack each. Specifically, the October figure represents a decline of 269 attacks compared with the previous month’s total of 367. This is just as the Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, assured Nigerians that the military would intensify efforts to apprehend those responsible for the attacks and bring them to justice. Oluyede also urged troops to remain disciplined, uphold the rules of engagement and respect human rights, while warning against complacency, particularly as the festive season approaches. He called on security agencies to strengthen intelligence sharing and joint planning, while urging community leaders and residents to report suspicious activities to security formations or through the military’s toll-free line, 193. Providing updates for Nigerians on military operations across the country, the Director, Defence Media Operations, Major-General Michael Onoja, revealed that many kidnapped victims would continue to be freed from captivity. “During the period under review, the AFN recorded a total of 98 attacks across various theatres of operation. Operation HADIN KAI recorded 27 attacks, Operation FANSAN YAMMA recorded 24, Operation ENDURING PEACE recorded 29, Operation WHIRL STROKE recorded 12, Operation UDO KA (OPUK) recorded 4, while Operation DELTA SAFE and Operation SAVANNAH SHIELD recorded 1 attack each,” the breakdown was contained in a document released on Friday. Earlier in September, Operation Enduring Peace recorded 147 attacks, Operation Fansan Yamma 115, Operation Whirl Stroke 55, Operation Hadin Kai 33, Operation Savannah Shield 13 and Operation Udo Ka four, while Operation Delta Safe recorded none. The senior military officer explained that troops neutralised more than 217 terrorists and criminals, arrested 333 suspects and rescued 349 kidnap victims during the month. item.content:encoded: Troops of the Nigerian military have drastically reduced attacks across various theatres of operations in October 2026, Daily Trust reports. Checks showed that only 98 attacks were recorded during the month under review, representing a 73.3 per cent decline from the 367 attacks recorded in September. A breakdown of the October figures showed that Operation Enduring Peace recorded the highest number of attacks with 29 incidents, followed by Operation Hadin Kai with 27 and Operation Fansan Yamma with 24. Operation Whirl Stroke recorded 12 attacks, while Operation Udo Ka recorded four. Operations Delta Safe and Savannah Shield recorded one attack each. Specifically, the October figure represents a decline of 269 attacks compared with the previous month’s total of 367. This is just as the Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede, assured Nigerians that the military would intensify efforts to apprehend those responsible for the attacks and bring them to justice. Oluyede also urged troops to remain disciplined, uphold the rules of engagement and respect human rights, while warning against complacency, particularly as the festive season approaches. He called on security agencies to strengthen intelligence sharing and joint planning, while urging community leaders and residents to report suspicious activities to security formations or through the military’s toll-free line, 193. Providing updates for Nigerians on military operations across the country, the Director, Defence Media Operations, Major-General Michael Onoja, revealed that many kidnapped victims would continue to be freed from captivity. “During the period under review, the AFN recorded a total of 98 attacks across various theatres of operation. Operation HADIN KAI recorded 27 attacks, Operation FANSAN YAMMA recorded 24, Operation ENDURING PEACE recorded 29, Operation WHIRL STROKE recorded 12, Operation UDO KA (OPUK) recorded 4, while Operation DELTA SAFE and Operation SAVANNAH SHIELD recorded 1 attack each,” the breakdown was contained in a document released on Friday. Earlier in September, Operation Enduring Peace recorded 147 attacks, Operation Fansan Yamma 115, Operation Whirl Stroke 55, Operation Hadin Kai 33, Operation Savannah Shield 13 and Operation Udo Ka four, while Operation Delta Safe recorded none. The senior military officer explained that troops neutralised more than 217 terrorists and criminals, arrested 333 suspects and rescued 349 kidnap victims during the month. He added that 70 insurgents surrendered to troops, while 105 arms and 3,174 rounds of ammunition were recovered. Onoja said the military also recovered 756,837 litres of stolen crude oil products and destroyed 49 illegal refining sites during operations against crude oil theft. “Throughout the month, over 217 terrorists and criminals were neutralized, with 333 terrorist/criminals arrested and 349 kidnap victims rescued. “Additionally, 70 insurgents surrendered to troops, while 105 arms and 3174 rounds of ammunition were recovered. “Similarly, the overall successes recorded in the fight against crude oil theft have continued to frustrate the activities of economic saboteurs, yielding the recovery of 756,837 litres of stolen crude oil products and destruction of 49 illegal refining sites. “Onoja said troops responded decisively to attacks recorded across the various theatres, engaging assailants with superior firepower and tactical manoeuvres to repel them,” he said. Terrorists surrender in droves in Northeast In the North East geopolitical zone, troops of Operation HADIN KAI sustained relentless operations against terrorism and its support networks across Adamawa, Borno, and Yobe States, with the Air Component providing decisive support. During the month, troops neutralized 162 terrorists and rescued 39 kidnap victims, arrested 98 terrorists, while 68 terrorists surrendered. A sustained wave of surrenders from terrorist enclaves was recorded throughout the month, with more than 50 terrorist fighters and their family members surrendering to troops at locations in Bama, Dikwa, Gwoza, Konduga, Mafa, and Monguno LGAs of Borno State. The surrendered persons consistently cited hunger, hardship, and violent clashes between rival terrorist factions as their reasons for fleeing. One suspect who surrendered to local security groups at Buni Gari in Gujba LGA of Yobe State on 17 October 2026 claimed to have been recruited through a social media group in 2024. In related operations, troops disrupted terrorist logistics and intelligence networks across the theatre. Suspected logistics suppliers, informants and collaborators were arrested at Tarmuwa and Kanama in Yobe State on 3 October 2026. Further arrests were made in Benisheikh, Damboa, Gubio, Monguno, and Ngurusoye between October 10th and 22nd, 2026. Between 23rd and 25th October 2026, troops also arrested a collector of illegal levies imposed by terrorists at Geidam market. Many kidnapped victims rescued in Northwest In the Northwest geopolitical zone, troops of Operation FANSAN YAMMA sustained offensive operations against terrorism, banditry and kidnapping throughout the month across Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto, and Zamfara States. The development has been denying terrorists freedom of action as troops intensified operations to disrupt terrorist support and logistics networks. During the month, troops neutralized 18 terrorists, rescued 167 kidnap victims, arrested 10 terrorists, while 1 terrorist surrendered. Troops gun down terrorists in North Central Troops of Operation SAVANNAH SHIELD sustained operations against terrorism and kidnapping across Kwara and Niger States. During the month, troops neutralized 3 terrorists, rescued 29 kidnap victims, arrested 3 terrorists, and facilitated the surrender of 1 terrorist. On October 10th, 2026, troops responded to the abduction of residents from farmlands in the Eruku-Egbe-Koro Forest area of Ekiti LGA of Kwara State and rescued 18 kidnapped persons. On 15 October 2026, troops at Bangi responded to a distress call of terrorists attempting to abduct farmers at Magaji Mai Kadarko Village, Bangi District, in Mariga LGA of Niger State. Troops engaged them and rescued 29 residents from nearby bushes, although one resident had regrettably been killed by the terrorists before the arrival of troops. Additionally, on 18 October 2026, a wanted terrorist kingpin and his accomplice at the kingpin’s residence were arrested in Mokwa town, Niger State, with efforts ongoing to apprehend other accomplices. In a related operations, on October 26th, 2026, troops on a fighting patrol to Latan Daji in Patigi LGA of Kwara State, neutralised two kidnappers and rescued five kidnapped victims. Meanwhile, the Joint Task Force, Operation WHIRL STROKE, has killed two suspected bandits in Kabba-Bunu and Lokoja Local Government Areas of Kogi State. Specifically, troops of Sector 3 of the JTF conducted the operation on Saturday, October 31, 2026, against suspected terrorists following an intelligence-led ambush along the Adankolo–Apata Road. “Acting on the intelligence, troops laid an ambush at suspected bandits’ supply route. The troops subsequently made contact with the suspected criminals who were subdued and forced to flee. “At about 0900 hours on the same day during exploitation, troops received information regarding the discovery of suspected bandits’ bodies towards Adankolo Forest. “On arrival at the location, troops found corpses of the two suspected bandits and recovered one locally made pistol, one cartridge and one empty case of 7.62mm special ammunition”, the military high command revealed.

item.title: Blue wave sweeps across America: 'In 1974, we had Watergate babies, now we have Iran War babies'
item.description: Stuart Norval welcomes France 24 International Affairs Editor Philip Turle and Hind Ziane, Geopolitical analyst and founder / CEO of Genpo. "In 1974, we had the Watergate babies. Now we have the Iran War babies," remarks Ziane with this striking historical analogy. Just as the Watergate scandal helped propel a new generation of Democratic lawmakers into Congress in 1974, Zian argues that public disillusionment with the Iran war, mounting economic pressures and dissatisfaction with Donald Trump's leadership may now be reshaping the American political landscape. Yet Turle reminds us, "They're not voting for Democrats because they love the Democrats. They're voting for the Democrats because they don't like Donald Trump."

item.title: ‘She can do what Beckham did’: Océane Hurtré making waves at Birmingham
item.description: WSL’s second-highest goalscorer is likened to England legend for her crossing and has earned France call-up At the conclusion of Birmingham’s warm-up, the players quietly and carefully placed their footballs into a draw-string bag. All except one, Océane Hurtré, who nonchalantly chipped hers straight into the bag from about 15 yards. It was an innocuous moment that might have escaped most onlookers at Hednesford Town’s Keys Park but it demonstrated the swagger with which she is playing. To observe the 22-year-old warming up before last week’s 1-1 League Cup draw at Aston Villa was to witness a player making skills look easy, taking one touch where others took two and pulling off no-look passes. She is backing up that panache in the Women’s Super League, as the joint-second-highest goalscorer with six from the promoted side’s opening eight matches. Only Khadija Shaw has scored more. Continue reading...

item.title: Drone warfare in space: Swarms of autonomous, laser-shooting cubesats could defend Western satellites in orbit
item.description:
Mark is an award-winning freelance aviation and space journalist and author of the non-fiction book "N-4 DOWN: The Hunt for the Arctic airship Italia." He began writing for Space.com in 2026 and writes for a range of publications, from BBC Future to The Smithsonian’s Air and Space Quarterly and others. Mark won awards two years in a row at the Aerospace Media Awards for features he had written on the history of drones and astronaut training. Space grabbed hold of Mark’s imagination when, as a child, he saw the opening scene of "Star Wars: A New Hope" for the first time and has never let go. Away from the final frontier, Mark can be found walking his dog along the country lanes of England’s Cotswolds.

In May 2026, four Russian military satellites came close to ICEYE-X36, a private synthetic aperture radar satellite widely believed to be providing battlefield intelligence for Ukraine, in an apparently aggressive and risky "grey zone" maneuver that spooked many in the space industry. Close enough to jam or interfere with the satellite's signal, blind it with a laser, fire a metal dart at it or, simply, force it to maneuver and burn fuel, the satellites' seemingly intimidatory behavior has increased the West's desire to develop defensive technology for satellites . In October 2026, it was reported that one of those same four Russian satellites passed within 500 meters (1,650 feet) of the same ICEYE satellite. Now, U.K. startup Shield Space is racing to apply the lessons of drone warfare in Ukraine to develop swarms of up to 100 very small, low-cost, attritable drone-like autonomous spacecraft called cubesats . Released by a car-sized carrier in Earth orbit, these microwave-sized spacecraft will act as interceptors to protect Western satellites , and their deployment will mark a next step in the evolution of orbital warfare . Shield Space says that these space drones will use "effectors" like lasers or microwaves, or "kinetic standoff" techniques, to defend Western satellites even if controllers lose contact with them. "We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million [$134 million US], which is how [much] you would pay for one satellite previously," said Graeme Ritchie, co-founder and CEO of Shield Space. Launched in 2023, NASA's civilian project Starling demonstrated that a swarm of four small satellites can cooperate and operate autonomously in space on a civilian science mission without relying heavily on real-time commands from ground control. But that seems like a far cry from the adversarial or defensive missions Shield Space and its competitors imagine. It is telling that the leading space powers appear not to have demonstrated swarm combat in space — although they tend to be reluctant to reveal their space warfare capabilities. In the fourth quarter of 2027, Shield Space plans to take this next step in space warfare's evolution by demonstrating rendezvous and prox
item.dc:creator: Mark Piesing
item.content:encoded:
Mark is an award-winning freelance aviation and space journalist and author of the non-fiction book "N-4 DOWN: The Hunt for the Arctic airship Italia." He began writing for Space.com in 2026 and writes for a range of publications, from BBC Future to The Smithsonian’s Air and Space Quarterly and others. Mark won awards two years in a row at the Aerospace Media Awards for features he had written on the history of drones and astronaut training. Space grabbed hold of Mark’s imagination when, as a child, he saw the opening scene of "Star Wars: A New Hope" for the first time and has never let go. Away from the final frontier, Mark can be found walking his dog along the country lanes of England’s Cotswolds.

In May 2026, four Russian military satellites came close to ICEYE-X36, a private synthetic aperture radar satellite widely believed to be providing battlefield intelligence for Ukraine, in an apparently aggressive and risky "grey zone" maneuver that spooked many in the space industry. Close enough to jam or interfere with the satellite's signal, blind it with a laser, fire a metal dart at it or, simply, force it to maneuver and burn fuel, the satellites' seemingly intimidatory behavior has increased the West's desire to develop defensive technology for satellites . In October 2026, it was reported that one of those same four Russian satellites passed within 500 meters (1,650 feet) of the same ICEYE satellite. Now, U.K. startup Shield Space is racing to apply the lessons of drone warfare in Ukraine to develop swarms of up to 100 very small, low-cost, attritable drone-like autonomous spacecraft called cubesats . Released by a car-sized carrier in Earth orbit, these microwave-sized spacecraft will act as interceptors to protect Western satellites , and their deployment will mark a next step in the evolution of orbital warfare . Shield Space says that these space drones will use "effectors" like lasers or microwaves, or "kinetic standoff" techniques, to defend Western satellites even if controllers lose contact with them. "We're talking about deploying 100 cubesats on a protect-and-defend mission for less than £100 million [$134 million US], which is how [much] you would pay for one satellite previously," said Graeme Ritchie, co-founder and CEO of Shield Space. Launched in 2023, NASA's civilian project Starling demonstrated that a swarm of four small satellites can cooperate and operate autonomously in space on a civilian science mission without relying heavily on real-time commands from ground control. But that seems like a far cry from the adversarial or defensive missions Shield Space and its competitors imagine. It is telling that the leading space powers appear not to have demonstrated swarm combat in space — although they tend to be reluctant to reveal their space warfare capabilities. In the fourth quarter of 2027, Shield Space plans to take this next step in space warfare's evolution by demonstrating rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) with two very small spacecraft. This effort, named Project Broadsword, will launch on SpaceX 's Transporter-21 rideshare mission. It will send up an 8U cubesat and a smaller 3U target craft, which Shield Space plans to maneuver from 100 kilometers (62 miles) apart to within 100 meters (330 feet) of each other and, through four stages of autonomy, from human-in-the-loop to "approximately" fully autonomous. (A cubesat unit, or U, is a cube that measures 10 cm, or about 4 inches, on a side.) Russia's Luch-2 satellite approaches another geostationary satellite on April 12, 2024, as tracked by the French company Aldoria's observation stations. (Image credit: Aldoria) The gaps between a true satellite-defense capability and this demonstration appear to be great, in terms of the technological and practical challenges of squeezing propulsion and power systems, AI compute power , sensors, the lasers the swarm needs to communicate and weapon systems onto small, lightweight maneuvering satellites. But it is a gap that Shield Space believes it can bridge through the purchase of relatively cheap off-the-shelf technology rather than more expensive bespoke designs. "Yes, it's a problem because of size, weight and power," Ritchie told Space.com. "We've had to totally innovate from scratch some elements of the mission… but we have only got roughly 100 cm by 100 cm [40 by 40 inches], so saving space or having systems that are already completely integrated is the main aim." "We have commissioned EnduroSat to build us an autonomous 8U cubesat that has chemical propulsion and its own imagery-collecting capability, which we will put our software on," said Dan Molland, co-founder and CTO of Shield Space, "and which we will then use to conduct our RPO . "The good thing about cubesats is they're very standardized and they're very off the shelf," he added. "There's always some level of adjusting you've got to do, but these cubesats are a lot more plug and play than more conventional platforms, which are usually all custom-built." Illustration of two Shield Space cubesats in orbit. (Image credit: Shield Space) Yet to focus on the technical issues may be to miss the point. "It takes an extraordinary amount of data to train the models and algorithms to achieve a fully autonomous mission," said Ritchie, "and the problem [unlike in the Ukraine war] is that data is not readily available. "We can train AI using synthetic data, but it's just not quite good enough for space. It's incredibly important to gather data from missions like this if we really want autonomous missions in the future." There is also the complexity of the AI needed in a war-fighting system. "Starling is a really great example," Molland told Space.com. "With Starling, you're essentially just asking a guidance system to make sure you stay within a given range of this or that satellite… But if you are controlling a swarm to deliver [a] military mission, you have a much more complex set of questions." It also comes with the challenge of ensuring that AI complies with any rules of engagement. But Ritchie and Molland believe these technical challenges can be overcome, and they have an aggressive schedule of demonstrations planned that they think will prove it. Bleddyn Bowen, associate professor of astropolitics at Durham University in the U.K. and author of the book "War in Space: Strategy, Spacepower, Geopolitics" (Edinburgh University Press, 2020), is more cautious about Shield Space's plans for the evolution of space warfare. "They remind me of a late Cold War missile-defense scheme called Brilliant Pebbles," he told Space.com. "It was one of the more advanced research and development programs in the Strategic Defense Initiative." The plan was to defend the U.S. against Soviet intercontinental ballistic missiles ( ICBMs ) by using thousands of small autonomous orbiting interceptors to destroy them by collision. "With enough investment, a lot is feasible," Bowen said. "But you're looking at many years of development and testing, solving the problem of testing kinetic weapons in space without leaving debris, and finding someone to buy the system." It is clear from Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine that the future of warfare includes swarms of low-cost autonomous drones — and Shield Space is already planning an aggressive schedule of missions to prove that this pattern applies to the final frontier as well. According to Ritchie, the startup hopes to quickly go from the first RPO demonstration to testing two full-sized 16U cubesats. It will then move on to a full carrier of 10 such cubesats, and then to a "super carrier" of 10 carriers, which will be deployed across multiple orbits. "We then get towards our future vision, which we call space-based carrier strike," said Ritchie. In this scenario, "responsive launch or pre-positioned carriers will give us an ability to protect and defend entire orbits, should you choose."
