"We designed [JWST] to be ready the moment an active interstellar comet was found and to follow it over time," Martin Cordiner of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Catholic University of America said in a statement . Cordiner leads the JWST program to study objects such as 3I/ATLAS, and he is a co-author on a new research paper describing some of the findings. The unclear origins of 3I/ATLAS Researchers know that 3I/ATLAS wasn't born in the solar system, but nobody knows around which star 3I/ATLAS formed. What scientists are more sure of is the fact that this interstellar comet was produced within a planet-forming disk of gas and dust around a young star, possibly as long ago as 10 to 12 billion years . That's over twice the age of our solar system. It was then ejected from its home system somehow and left to wander interstellar space before encountering our solar system. Like the familiar comets in our solar system, 3I/ATLAS is composed of grains of ice less than a micron – a millionth of a meter – in size. When the surface of the comet is warmed by the sun , gas erupts outwards, carrying ice grains into the cloud of ice and dust surrounding the comet, its coma, and its tail, where JWST can detect them. When viewed spectroscopically, the water-ice in comets native to our solar system creates a strong absorption line in a comet’s spectrum at a wavelength of three microns, as well as less-prominent absorption lines at 1.5 and two microns. Comparison between ice in the interstellar invader comet 3I/Atlas and icy bodies in our solar system. (Image credit: SwRI/Silvia Protopapa/NASA/ESA/CSA JWST) Yet when the JWST’s Near-Infrared spectrograph ( NIRSpec ) instrument viewed 3I/ATLAS three times between August 2025, before its closest approach to the sun, and after closest approach in April 2026, scientists found the 1.5- and two micron absorption lines were missing, though the three-micron line remained strong. "That combination was a puzzle," research lead author Silvia Protopapa of the South-west Research Institute said. "The strong three-micron band points to water-ice in the coma, but the weak or absent shorter-wavelength bands suggest the ice is not in the form we usually see in solar system comets ." The JWST's muddy 3I/ATLAS findings Whenever presented with an unusual observational signature such the JWST delievered for 3I/ATLAS researchers turn to modeling to find the physical characteristics that best fit the spectrum. The modeling suggested to Protopapa’s team that 3I/ATLAS was composed of sub-micron grains of dirty water-ice, rich in dust. In comparison, the grains from the solar system’s indigenous comets are much cleaner, with almost pure water-ice relatively uncontaminated by dust. "What seems to set [3I/ATLAS’ grains] apart is how much dust is mixed into the ice," said Protopapa. "Those grains hold clues to the conditions where the comet was born." The chemical composition of 3I/ATLAS (Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Martin Cordiner (CUA, NASA-GSFC); Image Processing: Alyssa Pagan (STScI)) Comets are made of primordial material found in the planet-forming disk of gas and dust that surrounds a young star, and therefore the composition of comets can provide a window into the conditions in which planets form. Whereas solar system comets tell us about the birth of Earth , an interstellar comet can tell us about conditions in which planets formed around another star, and how similar or dissimilar those conditions were to the birth of the solar system. Yet comets are not the only icy remnants that date back to such primordial times. There are various families of bodies in the outer solar system, and 3I/ATLAS’ spectrum bears a resemblance to the spectrum of some medium-sized TNOs that are rich in carbon-dioxide ice and organic compounds (organic meaning containing carbon atoms). Indeed, in a separate 2025 study led by Cordiner, the JWST found 3I/ATLAS to have one of the greatest abundances of carbon dioxide ever seen in a comet. TNOs are sizable bodies that are located far beyond the orbit of Neptune , The TNOs in question would have formed in a different part of the Sun’s protoplanetary disk than most comets and their composition reflects that. Artist's illustration of a planetary disk, a region of dust and gas where planets form. The zoom-in insert displays carbon monoxide molecules in the ice phase. (Image credit: M.Weiss/Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian) On the other hand, the results imply that 3I/ATLAS was formed around its star of origin from similar icy material to that which produced some of the TNOs in our solar system, showing that the building blocks of planets around other stars share a common range of properties with the building blocks that formed our solar system. Indeed, 3I/ATLAS could even be a fragment of a TNO-like body that was shattered in a collision. "At first glance, 3I/ATLAS looks different from the icy comets we know," said Protopapa. "But when we placed it alongside distant icy worlds in our own solar system, it no longer looked out of place. "This suggests that the icy building block of planets, here and around other stars, may share ice in the form of tiny, micron-scale grains, ranging from relatively pure ice to ice mixed with dust, with 3I/ATLAS toward the dusty end." What this tells us is that these sub-micron-sized icy grains must form first in planet-forming disks, to then be incorporated into large bodies such as comets and protoplanets. The team's findings were published on Monday (Oct. 26) in The Astrophysical Journal Letters .

item.title: Thieves pilfer environment variables from Trigger AI workflow tool
item.description: If you're a customer of cloud-hosted AI workflow platform Trigger.dev, take heed, because your environment variables may have been exposed in a security incident disclosed on Sunday. Trigger offered little explanation in its Sunday security incident report , noting that its investigation had identified “exposure across a subset of organizations” and that an attacker had gained unauthorized access to environment variables belonging to those organizations. Whatever exploit was used to gain access has been blocked, the company added, and affected customers have been notified of steps they need to take to prevent further security problems. We likely don't have to tell The Reg readers how important environment variables are in SaaS and cloud services like Trigger. If compromised environment variables contain sensitive credentials, an attacker could basically end up with the keys to the kingdom, potentially gaining access to connected services and digital infrastructure. For those unfamiliar with Trigger.dev, it’s a platform for building AI agents and workflows in TypeScript, but here’s the kicker: Trigger advertises itself as a durable execution platform that handles pesky things like retries, scaling, and keeping long-running tasks going through crashes and redeployments, while providing tools to monitor what those tasks are doing. Trigger, the company’s site notes, can be used to “build durable AI agents that survive refreshes, redeploys, and crashes,” and is ideal for “long-running tasks with retries, queues, AI observability and elastic scaling.” In short, companies running their AI on Trigger probably want it to keep running, which makes stolen environment variables all the more dangerous. Elastic scaling, automated retries, and, as Trigger notes, the ability to run lots of concurrent operations without timeouts could compound the consequences of compromised API keys, depending on what those credentials allow an attacker to access. An attacker with stolen credentials could potentially interfere with a customer's connected services or workflows. Additionally, Trigger recently added webhooks to its offering, supporting services like Stripe, Supabase, and Slack, potentially expanding the range of integrations that could be affected if their credentials were exposed. This could be pretty bad for anyone affected. Trigger has some fairly high-profile customers, with companies like fashion brand Emporio Armani, Pentagon-supporting AI acquisitions platform GovSignals, SaaS calendar platform Cal.com, and others all listed on the company’s site. Trigger has not publicly identified which organizations were affected by the intrusion. We reached out to Trigger, which declined to provide any additional information on the incident. A company spokesperson instead told us to wait for a full incident report to learn more. Luckily for Trigger customers and those concerned about SaaS security now that AI is regularly coming up with new vulnerabilities in commonly us

item.title: Token thieves costing companies $100K+ per day in illicit LLM charges
item.description: Victim organizations are losing millions of dollars in token charges as criminals hijack their corporate LLM access to steal expensive computing resources and AI services. These fraudulent charges from resource consumption can exceed $100,000 a day, according to a Monday report by Google's Mandiant incident responders, who saw cumulative charges at some organizations hit $1 million before the victim companies revoked intruders' access. "Whenever possible, threat actors want to use this technology to gain a scale advantage over defenders. They achieve that with agentic tools and by stealing tokens from unwitting third parties,” John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told The Register . “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks.” This tactic of hijacking access to LLMs is called LLMJacking , and it’s been increasing steadily over the past two years. In one extreme case, documented in an August report from CrowdStrike, a token thief sent about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. In one case detailed in the report, a group Google tracks as UNC6993 illicitly gained access to LLM API keys, then generated additional keys and enabled services within the victim’s cloud projects, racking up $100,000 in charges. The threat intel biz also documented a different token thief subscribing victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements to access advanced models on the victim company’s dime. The crook selected premium foundation models, launched high-volume inference streams, and used a “burn and rotate strategy” to bypass rate limits by creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the billing interface to monitor financial impact. In yet another incident, an intruder executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours using stolen third-party API keys to power a token routing service called Jet Night, according to a Monday report from Google. “Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably,” the report says. “For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month.” Jet Night has also admitted to multiple outages on its public Telegram channel, which the Google threat hunters note is “likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises.” Specialized LLMjacking roles As more criminals join the LLMJacking ecosystem, Google says it has documented a division of labor between the criminals that establish initial access to compromised cloud and AI services, and those that manage downstream monetization infrastructure, called “LLM Mixers.” In one case that Mandiant responded to in mid-2026,
item.dc:creator: Jessica Lyons
item.content:encoded: Victim organizations are losing millions of dollars in token charges as criminals hijack their corporate LLM access to steal expensive computing resources and AI services. These fraudulent charges from resource consumption can exceed $100,000 a day, according to a Monday report by Google's Mandiant incident responders, who saw cumulative charges at some organizations hit $1 million before the victim companies revoked intruders' access. "Whenever possible, threat actors want to use this technology to gain a scale advantage over defenders. They achieve that with agentic tools and by stealing tokens from unwitting third parties,” John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google Threat Intelligence Group, told The Register . “Locking down these resources will not only protect organizations from runaway costs, but also protect the broader community from a deluge of cheap, autonomous attacks.” This tactic of hijacking access to LLMs is called LLMJacking , and it’s been increasing steadily over the past two years. In one extreme case, documented in an August report from CrowdStrike, a token thief sent about 200,000 API requests in just two minutes. In one case detailed in the report, a group Google tracks as UNC6993 illicitly gained access to LLM API keys, then generated additional keys and enabled services within the victim’s cloud projects, racking up $100,000 in charges. The threat intel biz also documented a different token thief subscribing victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements to access advanced models on the victim company’s dime. The crook selected premium foundation models, launched high-volume inference streams, and used a “burn and rotate strategy” to bypass rate limits by creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the billing interface to monitor financial impact. In yet another incident, an intruder executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours using stolen third-party API keys to power a token routing service called Jet Night, according to a Monday report from Google. “Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably,” the report says. “For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month.” Jet Night has also admitted to multiple outages on its public Telegram channel, which the Google threat hunters note is “likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises.” Specialized LLMjacking roles As more criminals join the LLMJacking ecosystem, Google says it has documented a division of labor between the criminals that establish initial access to compromised cloud and AI services, and those that manage downstream monetization infrastructure, called “LLM Mixers.” In one case that Mandiant responded to in mid-2026, UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used this access to grant further access to a model API. The crooks also spun up a session hijacking page purporting to be an application portal to join a group of LLM users. “This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls,” the report says. Google predicts miscreants will “increasingly prioritize LLMJacking” compared to other types of resource theft like cryptojacking. And to prevent cloud LLM service abuse, the security firm says defenders should prioritize identity and access management plus supply chain security, and use a centralized secrets management platform to rotate keys and secrets. Also apply least-access privileges to users and service accounts, ensuring that they only have permissions necessary to complete their roles and tasks. And automate secrets scanning within codebases to identify and then remove any API keys and secrets added to source code. ®

item.title: Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: Sunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last season Sign up for our free newsletter here Arsenal are three points clear at the top of the Premier League table . But given the team in second are Manchester City, who are likely to be facing at the very least a major points deduction , perhaps more significant is that they are five clear of Brighton in third. The season of domination that many anticipated from the champions appears to be coming to pass. Liverpool challenged them on Sunday. There was a 20-minute spell before half-time when they swarmed all over Arsenal, and Anfield felt at least like it did in the golden years of Jürgen Klopp, when it buzzed with an energy that could overwhelm visitors. But Arsenal got through that, reset at half-time, and navigated the second half with relative comfort. For the second league game running, they denied Liverpool a shot on target. This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US. Subscribe for free here . Continue reading...

item.title: Led by Liam Rosenior and backed by billionaires, Paris FC are now a force in Ligue 1 | Luke Entwistle
item.description: After a huge summer and with PSG’s other rivals falling away, their city rivals are aiming to ‘be one of the biggest clubs in Europe’ By Get French Football News It is hard to know what Pierre Ferracci found stranger: the fact that he was fully suited among a set of bare-chested Paris FC ultras singing his name or that, behind him, in what was the final game of his presidency, his team were playing Monaco off the park. “I didn’t see any of the first 15 minutes of the game because I was with the ultras,” he admitted. On the pitch, as well as in the stands, was evidence of how far his side has come since he joined back in 2006. At that time, Les Parisiens were in the amateur third tier of French football. Ferracci arrived initially in an administrative function before becoming owner and president in 2012. It was not until 2017 that his side reached Ligue 2. Continue reading...

item.title: SUSE to cut one in ten employees because of... AI
item.description: One in ten employees at SUSE are facing the chop due to "automation and AI," according to a memo dispatched by management at the privately owned open source software biz. In an email to the 1,900 strong workforce on Monday - seen by The Register - CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen, the former Red Hat exec who joined SUSE in March 2023, confirmed the "difficult news." "We are announcing a reduction of SUSE’s global workforce of approximately 10 percent," he said. "These decisions are painful for our people, our culture, and our open source community, but they are necessary for us to adapt and build a sustainable, resilient SUSE for the long term." Van Leeuwen says the business, bought by Swedish private equity provider EQT, decided to cut jobs after scrutinizing its "future strategy, required capabilities, and team structures." The rest of the organization will get a look at the fiscal year 2027 strategy on November 16. He said in the message to staff: "What is clear is that automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate. AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work. We have seen this trend already both inside our sector and in the wider economy. This means that the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully. "We are adapting. Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years. This means we are accelerating investments in high priority areas, and deprioritizing others. These are hard, painful decisions to make, but necessary for our future." As The Reg reported in 2025, SUSE doubled down on AI . The specific roles at risk of redundancy were not outlined but SUSE claims it has considered where the people in those positions are "able to evolve, what they can stop doing, what they need to do more of - and decisions have been made on that basis." Staff caught up in the redundancies will be informed by November 4, employee representatives nominated the following day, and one to one meetings will begin at the start of next week. Van Leeuwen says in the internal memo that the job cuts are a "reflection of shifting organizational needs, not your talent or commitment. You have tackled hard infrastructure and open source challenges that power critical enterprise systems around the world. "Any organization will be fortunate to have your expertise." Back in September, we reported that the company was asking old hands if they would take "voluntary separation ." It seems not enough people chose to walk through the door, so instead, they're getting thrown through it instead. SUSE "geckos" in the Czech Republic may be glad they joined a trade union . Back in 2018, EQT bought SUSE from Microfocus for $2.5 billion. EQT floate

item.title: Football Daily | Aston Villa, ‘unacceptable insults’ and thin-skinned clutching of pearls
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! When Jamie Carragher appeared as a pundit on Sky Sports Super Sunday, Football Daily was surprised he didn’t have a solicitor sitting alongside him, occasionally jotting notes on a pad or leaning over to give whispered instructions and answer “no comment” to any leading questions about Trey Nyoni starting ahead of Ryan Gravenberch. On Friday night, the former Liverpool defender was subjected to a threat of legal action from Aston Villa, who took such grave exception to some “unacceptable insults” he had rained down on them from his podcast pulpit, that they were ready to call in the heavy legal artillery and stop him from preventing their “ascension in English and European football”. Taking a leaf out of the tried-and-much-ridiculed Nottingham Forest playbook , Villa chair Nassef Sawiris appears to have eschewed contacting Carragher through the usual formal channels and instead cajoled some unfortunate junior comms staffer to make the portentous announcement on their Social Media Disgraces. Continue reading...

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 2, 2000: Expedition 1 Arrives at the International Space Station
item.description: null On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents: NASA astronaut Bill Shepherd and two Russian cosmonauts, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev. The mission was called Expedition 1. Before this expedition, NASA had launched five, one-week-long Space Shuttle missions to help build the space station and bring up supplies. But this time, the crew would be staying for four and a half months, and they weren't taking the shuttle. Instead, they took a Russian Soyuz spacecraft , and this was the first Soyuz to ever dock at the space station. During their stay at the space station, they unpacked supplies and installed new equipment, including the first solar arrays. They left on the space shuttle Discovery, which brought up the Expedition 2 crew that would take their place. Expedition 1 crewmates Bill Shepherd, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev pose with a model of the space station as it appeared in 2000. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered As of today, there has been a continuous astronaut presence in space aboard the International Space Station for 26 years. For all of these years, not a day has gone by without someone living in space, orbiting our planet from aboard the space station. While the ISS was not the first space station, it has been the longest-running space statin by far. This first crew were pioneers, showing how humans could actually live and work aboard this station. This exploratory mission proved that the station could successfully support astronaut crews. Since this mission 26 years ago, there have been literally hundreds of astronauts from around the world who have flown to and lived aboard the ISS. While NASA has stated that the station might be decommissioned in the coming years, these accomplishments will remain forever in spaceflight history. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: A rainbow of ancient rocks on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 2, 2026
item.description: null In this image, we can see a colorful view of an ancient, rocky Martian hill. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UArizona) This rainbow-hued rocky plain looks like the landscape of an alien world. And, it turns out, it is. What is it? In this image, we can see an ancient, rocky hill on Mars . In the Red Planet's Southern Highlands, this alien terrain is chock-full of minerals, which we can see clearly defined in this color-enhanced view of the region. This image was snapped by the HiRISE camera aboard NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter ( MRO ), which has been studying the planet's surface, atmosphere and climate since arriving in Martian orbit in March 2006. But this isn't exactly what the surface of the planet would look like through our eyes; the image is color-enhanced. Why would scientists take a natural-color image and turn it rainbow? Doing so enhances the slight color differences in these rocks, allowing researchers to pick out the different minerals. Why is it incredible? As pointed to above, enhancing colors in scientific images can be an incredibly useful tool for exploration. For instance, in this image, the blue- and green-toned rocks could be full of minerals like pyroxenes and olivine, according to scientists analyzing the image. And they think that the yellow, orange and red patches may contain minerals formed by past interactions with liquid water. By exploring the mineral content of rocks like this, researchers can peel back the layers of history within the Martian bedrock. The discovery of certain minerals, for example, can show that water flowed on Mars long ago, pointing to potentially habitable conditions . So, as we can see, this striking rainbow image isn't just a beautiful landscape; it's also hiding serious clues to Mars' history.

item.title: Nuclear threats and street brawls: Russia, Ukraine report attacks on their emergency alert apps
item.description: Cyberattacks on both Russia’s and Ukraine’s emergency alert apps resulted in fake messages about missile and nuclear strikes broadcast to the public. Officials from both countries confirmed the attacks, which occurred at similar times, on Sunday evening. According to public statements and messages sent via social media, Ukraine’s alert app was hit first, with the country’s Air Force quick to dispel nuclear fears. "The Air Alert app has likely been compromised," it said via Telegram at around 2100 UTC. "There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel!" At around 0030 UTC on Monday, Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations confirmed the country’s app had also been abused, with fake messages sent to citizens' devices. "Attention! The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations' mobile app has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public," it said, also via Telegram. "Work is currently underway to patch the vulnerability and restore normal operation." The ministry issued an update around 90 minutes later, saying the app was once again functioning normally, and pointing out that an attack on the app was not the same as a compromise of the state’s national alert system. "Citizens are alerted through primary channels: regional and municipal alert systems (sirens, loudspeakers), communication networks (SMS messaging), and television and radio broadcasts. The mobile app is merely an additional, supporting information service," it stated. Ukraine's Ministry of Digital Affairs also issued a public announcement reminding citizens about how to receive emergency warnings while its “Alarm!” app was down. These include enabling iOS and Android emergency alerts, state-controlled sirens, and other official sources, such as the official social media accounts of Ukraine's government. According to the messages sent to devices after the compromise of Ukraine's alert app, the fake warnings pertained to various threats, such as street fights in Kyiv, chemical attacks, and radiation hazards. Alerts about the threat of nuclear fallout from official government warning systems would normally lead to panic, however, one of the earliest messages sent to citizens was written in Russian and referenced the "Oreshnik" missile, which was an immediate signal that the message may not be genuine. Equivalent alerts sent to Russian citizens also warned of impending nuclear strikes "at all regions of Russia," referencing "P1-Sun," the name of a Ukrainian attack drone. Oleksander Merezhko, who chairs the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee and noted the suspicious Russian-language alert, told the BBC the attack was almost certainly part of Russia's cyber war . "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that," he said. "It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities." Russia has not explicitly blamed Ukraine for the attack on its app,

item.title: Microsoft's Canada timezone troubles leave admins fixing calendars, pretending they're in Bogota
item.description: Microsoft has discovered once again that few things strike fear into the heart of a software engineer quite like a government deciding to fiddle with the clocks. Parts of Canada stopped observing seasonal clock changes on November 1, leaving affected areas of British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba permanently on UTC-07:00, UTC-06:00 and UTC-05:00 respectively. Unfortunately, Microsoft's sprawling software empire hasn't entirely caught up. The company has confirmed problems across a chunk of its software estate, leaving some customers facing incorrect times, broken schedules and a collection of workarounds while Redmond catches up. Outlook users have been left with the most homework. Switching to the new Canadian time zones won't automatically update existing calendar entries, meaning that meetings scheduled after November 1 are potentially an hour out of whack. Microsoft advises users to change their Outlook calendar time zone, then update upcoming events and meetings to use it. For meetings involving other people, only the organizer can make the change. Recurring meetings come with an additional treat: changing the time zone resets any previously moved occurrences, which then have to be recreated. Anyone with a calendar full of recurring meetings may wish to put the kettle on first. Microsoft is working on an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet to remediate non-recurring meetings, but according to its guidance, that's not due until later this week. A fix for recurring meetings remains "in development," with an ETA yet to be confirmed. Things get stranger with Power Automate and Fabric, where Microsoft's temporary fix involves pretending you're somewhere else entirely. Depending on the product and province, that could mean Saskatchewan, Arizona or, for Manitobans, Bogota. Because apparently time zones weren't confusing enough already. SharePoint On-Prem customers, meanwhile, have to wait until November 10 for the correct time zones to arrive, while Power Pages users could see server-formatted dates appear an hour out until a service fix lands. Microsoft's current milestone for that is December 12. Admins dealing with the fallout aren't exactly delighted. One sysadmin on Reddit said Microsoft's guidance had been "terrible" and claimed to have written roughly 900 lines of PowerShell to change users' Outlook settings and manually adjust calendar events. Others described switching systems to Saskatchewan time while waiting for Microsoft's new zones to settle in. Microsoft published its guidance on October 26, less than a week before the change took effect, and was still adding affected products and workarounds four days later. Meanwhile, admins were urged to test calendars, recurring meetings, and schedules before the November 1 switch, leaving little time to find out what might break. If any of this sounds familiar, it's because time has caused trouble for Microsoft before . In 2022, Chile delayed its switch to daylight saving time by a week. Microso

Microsoft responded by warning that Windows clocks could be wrong, scheduled tasks could run at unexpected times, and timestamps on files, transactions, and logs could end up an hour out. Four years later, governments are still messing with time and software is still apparently objecting. ®

item.title: From VHS dreams to San Siro glory: Amorim’s Milan surge puts rivals on notice | Nicky Bandini
item.description: Inspired by the legendary Milan sides of his youth, the manager gave his side a lift with a tactical victory over Inter Ruben Amorim had waited a lifetime for his first Milan derby. As a kid growing up in Lisbon, he supported two football teams. There was the local one, Benfica, whose games he attended so early in life that his father has recalled changing nappies in the stands of the old Estádio da Luz. And the other one that captivated him from overseas. “I remember watching tapes of that Milan team with [Paolo] Maldini, [Franco] Baresi, [Ruud] Gullit, [Frank] Rijkaard, [Dejan] Savicevic,” Amorim told the Portuguese newspaper Expresso in 2017. “My childhood dreams were to play for Benfica and Milan. I’ve fulfilled one. Now I suppose I’ll have to become a coach for the other!” Continue reading...

item.title: Frozen part II: Hackers remotely defrost produce in Euro supermarkets ... again
item.description: The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food wastage as a result of miscreants raising the temperatures to highs of 50ºC (122°F). In Belgium, around 40 Delhaize stores were affected after the attackers reportedly switched fridges and freezers into defrost mode overnight, between Sunday and Monday, resulting in stock issues. Diego Louwers, a Proxy Delhaize store manager in Overijse, near Brussels, told RTL Info that the consequences of the cyberattacks were "catastrophic," forcing the store to throw out the entirety of its fresh and frozen products. "We can't have anything worse in our line of work," he said. "We have to throw away all of our merchandise, and it's both heartbreaking and very complicated operationally." A Delhaize spokesperson said it took steps to ensure stores remain stocked, although fresh and frozen products are "temporarily somewhat limited." "On Monday, 2 November, we identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen of our stores," they said. "We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational and ensure that our customers can continue to do their shopping as usual. "In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centres are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores. "We are, of course, continuing to ensure that our products are stored and presented under optimal conditions, so that we can provide our customers with the quality and freshness they have come to expect from us." Around 15 Carrefour stores are also reportedly affected, as are sites operated by Intermarché, Spar, and Shop & Go stores located at Q8 service stations. Belgium’s De Laet & Van Haver chain of butcher shops reported temperature rises in its appliances too, but followed up with a statement on Monday saying there was no impact on its produce, and all stores remain open. Simultaneously, similar issues have affected Swedish grocery chain ICA, which confirmed attacks on a "small number of stores." "We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network," a company spokesperson said. "The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation." ICA did not respond to questions about the scale of food wastage nor when normal operations are expected to continue. One store, ICA Nära in Böda on Öland, said via social media that it is open today but has no fresh or frozen produce to sell. "Unfortunately, we are one of the stores whose refrigerators and freezers have been hacked," it said. "We are open as usual, but unfortunately we have no refrigerators and freezers to sell. item.content:encoded: The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food wastage as a result of miscreants raising the temperatures to highs of 50ºC (122°F). In Belgium, around 40 Delhaize stores were affected after the attackers reportedly switched fridges and freezers into defrost mode overnight, between Sunday and Monday, resulting in stock issues. Diego Louwers, a Proxy Delhaize store manager in Overijse, near Brussels, told RTL Info that the consequences of the cyberattacks were "catastrophic," forcing the store to throw out the entirety of its fresh and frozen products. "We can't have anything worse in our line of work," he said. "We have to throw away all of our merchandise, and it's both heartbreaking and very complicated operationally." A Delhaize spokesperson said it took steps to ensure stores remain stocked, although fresh and frozen products are "temporarily somewhat limited." "On Monday, 2 November, we identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen of our stores," they said. "We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational and ensure that our customers can continue to do their shopping as usual. "In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centres are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores. "We are, of course, continuing to ensure that our products are stored and presented under optimal conditions, so that we can provide our customers with the quality and freshness they have come to expect from us." Around 15 Carrefour stores are also reportedly affected, as are sites operated by Intermarché, Spar, and Shop & Go stores located at Q8 service stations. Belgium’s De Laet & Van Haver chain of butcher shops reported temperature rises in its appliances too, but followed up with a statement on Monday saying there was no impact on its produce, and all stores remain open. Simultaneously, similar issues have affected Swedish grocery chain ICA, which confirmed attacks on a "small number of stores." "We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network," a company spokesperson said. "The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation." ICA did not respond to questions about the scale of food wastage nor when normal operations are expected to continue. One store, ICA Nära in Böda on Öland, said via social media that it is open today but has no fresh or frozen produce to sell. "Unfortunately, we are one of the stores whose refrigerators and freezers have been hacked," it said. "We are open as usual, but unfortunately we have no refrigerators and freezers to sell. "We have no status on when the refrigerators and freezers are expected to be up and running again." The store manager, Mats Olsson, told SVT that he arrived to work on Monday morning and was greeted by a puddle of water and freezers set to 55 degrees C – a tale echoed by other managers across the country. Coop stores are affected by similar attacks too, with six locations in central Sweden experiencing fridge-freezer issues, according to a company spokesperson. Likewise, at least 13 SuperValue stores in Ireland are also affected, with fresh and frozen food being thrown out, according to parent company Musgrave speaking to RTE . The news comes less than a month after various grocery chains in France resorted to discarding bucketfuls of produce after their appliances were remotely defrosted by cybercrooks . Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others were hit with cyberattacks in mid-October, and hundreds of stores across the chains were reportedly impacted. At least some of the affected stores were running outdated firmware on their Danfoss refrigeration controllers, and shortly after the attacks were confirmed, CERT-FR published an alert pertaining to numerous Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controller compromises . Other retailers, such as Coopérative U, confirmed they were not Danfoss customers. It remains unclear if the latest attacks across Europe used the same methods as those used for the disruption in France last month. None of the companies that spoke to The Register on Monday responded to questions about who was behind the intrusions. ®

item.title: 'VisionQuest' homework guide: Everything you need to watch to understand Marvel's WandaVision follow-up
item.description: null Marvel Studios' existential superhero series " VisionQuest " has arrived on Disney+, and we've already been treated to four intriguing episodes that delve into the complex life of Vision, Paul Bettany's intelligent android and former card-carrying member of The Avengers. The staggered storyline leading up to this show began with 2021's " WandaVision " and the 2024 follow-up, "Agatha All Along," with Marvel Studios proclaiming "VisionQuest" to be "the final vision of the groundbreaking trilogy." So, for those trying to catch up on current events in this trilogy of MCU shows starring Vision, and to avoid any lingering confusion, let’s take a step back to fill in the gaps. And now, this isn't as simple as just "watch all the Marvel movies and shows in order," because that is a frankly ridiculous undertaking and entirely too much homework to do before watching a show. We're distilling it down to just what you need to know to understand VisionQuest. Spoiler warning: It should go without saying, but there are spoilers for previous Marvel movies and shows in this article. You have been warned! TLDR: Marvel shows and movies you need to watch ahead of VisionQuest We'll go into some detail on all the connections below, but if you just want a list of the essential Marvel shows and movies to watch before VisionQuest, here it is. Note that this is just the essentials. There are loads of small references to other movies and shows in the MCU, but they're just nods. Avengers: Age of Ultron Avengers: Infinity War WandaVision Doctor Strange and the Multiverse of Madness* Agatha All Along *This one is debatable. It continues Wanda's story from WandaVision, but it's not really essential for understanding the events of VisionQuest. Both are the true vision. Neither is the true Vision (Image credit: Disney / Marvel) We kick things off with 2018's "Avengers: Infinity War," where the mighty Thanos murdered Vision by plucking out his golden, forehead-mounted Mind Stone for his Infinity Gauntlet. From that moment forward, Vision was dead, and Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) was cast into unfathomable grief and not-so-repressed anger. From there, we pick up the story in the 2021 Disney+ series "WandaVision." Set weeks after "Avengers: Endgame," this show features two separate versions of Vision. One was a new synthezoid version, Frankensteined together from the components of the old Vision by S.W.O.R.D., nicknamed White Vision. The other Vision is a supernatural manifestation, brought to life via Wanda Maximoff’s sorcery; he is known as Hex Vision. White Vision is ready to rumble in "VisionQuest" (Image credit: Disney+) So, which of these two Visions appears in "VisionQuest"? That's the fun (and confusing) part, because the answer is both of them. At the end of "WandaVision," Hex Vision restores the lost memories of White Vision, essentially merging two entities into one. item.dc:creator: Jeff Spry
item.content:encoded: null Marvel Studios' existential superhero series " VisionQuest " has arrived on Disney+, and we've already been treated to four intriguing episodes that delve into the complex life of Vision, Paul Bettany's intelligent android and former card-carrying member of The Avengers. The staggered storyline leading up to this show began with 2021's " WandaVision " and the 2024 follow-up, "Agatha All Along," with Marvel Studios proclaiming "VisionQuest" to be "the final vision of the groundbreaking trilogy." So, for those trying to catch up on current events in this trilogy of MCU shows starring Vision, and to avoid any lingering confusion, let’s take a step back to fill in the gaps. And now, this isn't as simple as just "watch all the Marvel movies and shows in order," because that is a frankly ridiculous undertaking and entirely too much homework to do before watching a show. We're distilling it down to just what you need to know to understand VisionQuest. Spoiler warning: It should go without saying, but there are spoilers for previous Marvel movies and shows in this article. You have been warned! TLDR: Marvel shows and movies you need to watch ahead of VisionQuest We'll go into some detail on all the connections below, but if you just want a list of the essential Marvel shows and movies to watch before VisionQuest, here it is. Note that this is just the essentials. There are loads of small references to other movies and shows in the MCU, but they're just nods. Avengers: Age of Ultron Avengers: Infinity War WandaVision Doctor Strange and the Multiverse of Madness* Agatha All Along *This one is debatable. It continues Wanda's story from WandaVision, but it's not really essential for understanding the events of VisionQuest. Both are the true vision. Neither is the true Vision (Image credit: Disney / Marvel) We kick things off with 2018's "Avengers: Infinity War," where the mighty Thanos murdered Vision by plucking out his golden, forehead-mounted Mind Stone for his Infinity Gauntlet. From that moment forward, Vision was dead, and Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) was cast into unfathomable grief and not-so-repressed anger. From there, we pick up the story in the 2021 Disney+ series "WandaVision." Set weeks after "Avengers: Endgame," this show features two separate versions of Vision. One was a new synthezoid version, Frankensteined together from the components of the old Vision by S.W.O.R.D., nicknamed White Vision. The other Vision is a supernatural manifestation, brought to life via Wanda Maximoff’s sorcery; he is known as Hex Vision. White Vision is ready to rumble in "VisionQuest" (Image credit: Disney+) So, which of these two Visions appears in "VisionQuest"? That's the fun (and confusing) part, because the answer is both of them. At the end of "WandaVision," Hex Vision restores the lost memories of White Vision, essentially merging two entities into one. So, the Vision we see in "VisionQuest" is the physical body of White Vision, injected with thoughts and remembrances of the model that was magically resurrected by Wanda. Confused yet? Don't worry, it's going to get weirder. Voices inside my head The great James Spader as Ultron's avatar in "VisionQuest" (Image credit: Disney+) In addition to the two versions of Vision from "WandaVision," numerous other AIs exist within Vision's skull and are all represented by human avatars acting as factions of his ravaged psyche. Cast your mind all the way back to 2015's "Avengers: Age of Ultron," and you'll remember that Vision was conceived from a combination of the artificial brain of Ultron, the Mind Stone, and fragments of Tony Stark’s AI butler companion, J.A.R.V.I.S., who was named after the real Jarvis seen in the "Agent Carter" TV series. J.A.R.V.I.S. appears in "VisionQuest" as his own unique entity, alongside another of Tony Stark's AI helpers, E.D.I.T.H., aka the AI in the smart glasses that Stark left to Peter Parker after his death. She shows up in "Spider-Man: Far From Home," which is a great movie but not an essential viewing if you're preparing for "VisionQuest." Then let's toss in the fact that papa Ultron (James Spader) is buzzing around in Vision’s cranium, creating what’s been described as more or less an "Age of Ultron" and a "WandaVision" sequel at the same time. As it turns out, Vision did not destroy Ultron at the end of "Age of Ultron"; he copied his code and absorbed him, so now the rabid robot lives on in Vision’s brain. Like father, like son Paul Bettany stars as Vision in Disney+'s engaging new superhero series, "VisionQuest" (Image credit: Disney+) The show’s narrative is centered around the complicated relationship between Vision and his son Tommy Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). Tommy was created by Wanda's Hex and should have disappeared when it collapsed, but both he and his brother Billy survived through magical shenanigans that are explained in 2024's "Agatha All Along." Those two Maximoff boys, Tommy and Billy, both vanished from existence at the conclusion of "WandaVision." "Agatha All Along" exposed the truth that their consciousnesses entered the ether before expiring, only to reemerge into the souls of two teenage boys who had just perished, therefore returning them to life. Are you still with us? Good, just checking. The finale of "Agatha All Along" hinted at the return of the estranged Tommy, and "VisionQuest" dives into that dangling plot point with relish! Palad-in for a bad time (Image credit: Disney / Marvel) Every show needs an antagonist, and the voices in Vision's head can't do all the work. "VisionQuest" has introduced a duo of villains for Vision to contend with. Neither of them has shown up in the MCU previously, though, so you don't need to do any research here. With a massive bounty on his head after breaking free from S.W.O.R.D.'s control, White Vision must contend with a new villainous foe in the form of a mysterious mercenary named Paladin (Todd Stashwick). This enigmatic Marvel Comics character was created by Jim Shooter and Carmine Infantino and was first seen prowling the pages of "Daredevil #150" back in 1978. He's basically a gun-for-hire in the Marvel universe, often hired to fight alongside or against various heroes depending on the story. We don't know much about his motivations in the show, but we'll learn more as it goes on. "VisionQuest" also shines a spotlight on the bizarro character of Ultron's "bride," Jocasta, though the MCU version of this character diverges wildly from the comic book inspiration. (Image credit: Disney / Marvel) It's enough to drive one to madness! Between all the father-son dynamics dancing around the eight scheduled episodes, being hunted down by mercs, and his transcendent search for meaning, Vision and his saga are hopefully headed to a peaceful end. Created by Terry Matalas ("Star Trek: Picard," "12 Monkeys") and airing two new chapters each Tuesday night on Disney+, VisionQuest is bolstered by a cast that includes Ruaridh Mollica, T'Nia Miller, Lauren Morais, Orla Brady, Diane Morgan, Polly Frame, Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, Emily Hampshire, and James D’Arcy. Watch VisionQuest on Disney+: Disney+ (With Ads): $11.99/month Disney+ Premium (No Ads): $18.99/month or $189.99/year

item.title: Anthropic's IPO prospectus is big on promises, short on answers to tough questions
item.description: It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Man n and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode. For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors. In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is. A lightly edited transcript is below: Brandon (00:03) Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register 's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're focusing on what I think our contributor Carly Page aptly described as the peak of the AI hype cycle we've been in for the past few years, and that's the public release of Anthropic's initial public offering filing. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter. Welcome guys. Tobias Mann (00:34) Good to be here. Tom Claburn (00:34) Good to be here. Brandon (00:36) So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb . Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO. Tobias Mann (00:56) Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy. Brandon (01:18) Right. Tobias Mann (01:18) The S-1 definitely did that. But on the numbers side of things, the takeaway for the market was kind of interesting because there were some people looking at the numbers and going, "OK, this actually seems reasonable." Their operating losses were only about 700 million dollars. Brandon (01:40) I think on 16.3 billion net [revenues], right? That was what they reported. Tobias Mann (01:46) Right. Brandon (01:47) Now they also mentioned, I think, and I was going to ask you about this, $80.7 billion total losses, but I understand that was an accounting adjustment of some kind. Did they mention in the IPO what that meant specifically? Tobias Mann (02:01) Not specifica

item.content:encoded: It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music , or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Man n and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode. For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors. In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is. A lightly edited transcript is below: Brandon (00:03) Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register 's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're focusing on what I think our contributor Carly Page aptly described as the peak of the AI hype cycle we've been in for the past few years, and that's the public release of Anthropic's initial public offering filing. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter. Welcome guys. Tobias Mann (00:34) Good to be here. Tom Claburn (00:34) Good to be here. Brandon (00:36) So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb . Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO. Tobias Mann (00:56) Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy. Brandon (01:18) Right. Tobias Mann (01:18) The S-1 definitely did that. But on the numbers side of things, the takeaway for the market was kind of interesting because there were some people looking at the numbers and going, "OK, this actually seems reasonable." Their operating losses were only about 700 million dollars. Brandon (01:40) I think on 16.3 billion net [revenues], right? That was what they reported. Tobias Mann (01:46) Right. Brandon (01:47) Now they also mentioned, I think, and I was going to ask you about this, $80.7 billion total losses, but I understand that was an accounting adjustment of some kind. Did they mention in the IPO what that meant specifically? Tobias Mann (02:01) Not specifically. It's a little fuzzy, and it's always kind of like this. Brandon (02:07) Of course it is, right? Tobias Mann (02:09) Anthropic's business is extremely cash heavy, and so they had to go to partners and say, "Hey, we need capital in order to pay for compute to train these models. We can either take it in debt or you could also get repaid in valuation, our equity." And so I believe a large part of that loss is they're trying to write off a lot of the equity that they're going to have to pay off when they do go public. And so I do believe that's the lion's share of that loss. Because it does look huge, but when you think about how companies go public and how they raise capital as startups, it's not really that surprising. It's just a huge number because Anthropic is arguably the largest IPO in US history at this point. Brandon (03:02) Right. But bottom line is their actual day-to-day business losses were $693 million....It was $1.2 billion, I think, for the first half of the year or same time last year or something like that. So it's gone down. Tobias Mann (03:17) Yes. Tom Claburn (03:17) And they're trying to go out at two trillion now? Is that the number? Tobias Mann (03:25) Well, the number kind of depends on whether they're going to be able to sustain this. I was going to mention for the first time ever, their revenues outpaced their compute expenses two to one. This has never been true in the company's history, and it's one of the reasons that people are feeling more confident about this. The issue that really comes from all of this, and what has gotten missed somewhat in the more rosy interpretations of the S-1, is that they also are signed up to have to repay upwards of 800 billion dollars and counting of compute commitments out through the next two decades or so. Brandon (04:12) You outlined in your story just a whole host of people they owed billions of dollars to for compute. Like you said, it would be great. That $16.3 billion in [revenue] would be great if those compute costs were going to hold steady, right? But they're not. They're going to keep climbing and there are a lot of bills that are going to be due. So, profitability is relying on making more than that nearly trillion dollars in compute obligations, and that's a big if. Tom Claburn (04:43) I mean, the big question mark is in terms of what the technology does for inference costs, because I think a lot of this is betting on being able to get the same hardware that is much more efficient down the road and maybe not drop your prices proportionately and profit on the difference. But it remains to be seen whether there will be enough competition to just have the price go do with the increasing cost. And you see that a lot. I think the inference costs have dropped pretty significantly over the year, on average. I mean, it's really hard to calculate inference costs because there are so many different factors and it's really situational depending on the workload and how much caching is going on and things like that. But overall it's a lot cheaper to do inference now than it was a few months ago. Tobias Mann (05:34) Per token, yeah. Brandon (05:36) But again, I feel like if you're betting this $2 trillion IPO on the fact that we're going to keep getting better and cheaper at inference, right? I mean, I know Moore's Law is kind of a thing of the past, but at this point, what if we run up against another compute bottleneck and inference stops getting cheaper before they need it to? Obviously any IPO prospectus is one big document about risk, right? Like, "Hey, you might make a ton of money investing in this company, or we might go complete belly up and you lose everything," right? That's always a possibility. Tom Claburn (06:15) Right. And they still haven't demonstrated that the use case for AI is wide enough at volume that they claim it is. I mean, in certain sectors it's pretty obvious now there's going to be AI for a long time. Coding, everyone kind of agrees that works and we know how to manage that. And then there will be adjacent fields to that. But once you start getting into more general office work and regular business tasks that are not super-compute heavy, I don't know. It's a good question. We'll see if people are going to use it that broadly, but I just see it being overly optimistic. Tobias Mann (06:59) The big question I have right now is: Is there enough user demand to support even a $200 billion a year revenue stream? Because even going off just commitments that they can't get out of made in the first half of this year, that's $417 billion running out through about 2033 to 2036. Brandon (07:32) I think the upper end of your estimate was a total, including newer commitments, of about $807 billion. At the lower end, $782 billion at the lower end. That's not that much of a difference when you're looking at hundreds of billions of dollars. Tobias Mann (07:46) But if they can't

item.title: Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or party gives way to anxiety-filled hangover for Bayern Munich | Andy Brassell
item.description: Dortmund did not read the script, remaining level on points with the defending champions at the top of the table It was the moment they had all been … not so much waiting for, but planning, pushing and yearning for. In the videos that announce the starting lineup on the giant scoreboard before kick-off, every Bayern Munich player turns to face the camera with their personal salute, greeting or goal celebration, the playful progression from the standard folding of arms. Except on Saturday evening, the No 9 turned around smiling, and cradling the golden trophy. In the midweek DFB Pokal stroll against Magdeburg there had been a salute, the players welcoming Harry Kane on to the pitch with a guard of honour to commemorate his Ballon d’Or victory two nights before. This, however, was the real party, the moment where the England captain’s and Bayern’s successful union and the apex it has reached was celebrated in front of a global audience. There was every reason to believe it would be a full and satisfying victory lap, even in Der Klassiker, with proper competition so often bringing the best out of the Rekordmeister. Continue reading...

Madam-carer, just let me be,” I grunted, picking up pebbles and tossing them back into the water. “No, seriously, I care about you. You left home claiming to go to your Alternative Therapist, yet look at you sitting by the beach playing with sand like a kindergartener,” Lantana said. “Lantana, please, do you mind? I really need my space right now.” “Abeg shift joor! Aunty lone-ranger. Every time you need your space, you need your space; you no dey tire of yourself?” “No, ma. I am still my best company.” “Very boring. How a human being can stay alone and claim that they are having fun by themself baffles me.” Lantana sits beside me and nudges closer. I side-eye her and shift aside. She moves closer. I sidle away; she comes closer and drapes her right leg across mine with a twinkle in her eyes. “Babe, free me na. I came here to breathe.” I begged. “You came here to breathe? Egbami, you been dey suffocate before? You left home to go to Iwona’s for therapy, so how did you now end up at the beach? “She say she get another customer.” I picked up a smooth pebble and a coral and lay back on the sand. “I no understand. She get another customer bi bawo? Didn’t you book this slot?” “I did.” “So, which kain talk be that?” Lantana was bristling already. “I was running late and sent her a message.” “You were running late? You ran from your house to here across three postcodes? With which strength abi you wan kpai?” Lantana looked worried. “Gaskiya, Lantana, you no get sense. Run as in how na? Shey today na Parkrun ni? I say I come late.” “Aha! That is what you should say na, auntie. You know you runners, once you say run, we take it literally.” “So, I go run the 22 miles because I want to prove what?” I glared at her. “Ah, a le so! You left home to go to Iwona’s for therapy, so how did you now end up at the beach? “She say she get another customer.” I picked up a smooth pebble and a coral and lay back on the sand. “I no understand. She get another customer bi bawo? Didn’t you book this slot?” “I did.” “So, which kain talk be that?” Lantana was bristling already. “I was running late and sent her a message.” “You were running late? You ran from your house to here across three postcodes? With which strength abi you wan kpai?” Lantana looked worried. “Gaskiya, Lantana, you no get sense. Run as in how na? Shey today na Parkrun ni? I say I come late.” “Aha! That is what you should say na, auntie. You know you runners, once you say run, we take it literally.” “So, I go run the 22 miles because I want to prove what?” I glared at her. “Ah, a le so! We never can tell with weirdos like you.” She shot me a sly grin. “Lantana, I can’t deal right now. Just free me; let me breathe.” “So you came late? How many minutes late?” “26 minutes.” “Haba, that is so unlike you. What happened?” “I tried to catch the 3:15 bus but missed it. Then walked 15 minutes to the next bus stop, and the bus was delayed for 10 minutes. I decided to walk to the next one so I could catch a direct bus to her place, but that bus stop was closed. I went to the next one.” “Johnny Walka. Why didn’t you simply take a cab? See as you punish yourself on top £20.” “I no bi God na. I no see say na so e go bẹ.” I stood up, stretched and began walking into the waters. “Babe, you wan jump inside water? No koba mẹ o,” she screeched. “Olódò ni e. Jump say wetin happen? Say she save money wey I for pay the therapist?” “Wow, that is awesome. Look how you reframed it already. Instead of you to say you miss your wellbeing session, you said she miss money.” “Isn’t that the truth? She just missed this £50 quid. I will see if I can book with the other Polish woman at my àdúgbò or maybe try that Egyptian guy for acupuncture. Been a long time since I went to him.” “But that Polish woman is more expensive, isn’t she?” Lantana cocked a brow. By now she was standing by the bank of the ocean, still kicking sand. Her morbid aquaphobia meant she wouldn’t dare come in. “Yeah. She charges £50 for 30 minutes. While this babe dey collect same amount for an hour.” “Ọmọ, see levels! Why the margin? Na gold dust she dey use?” “Sebi I tell you say you no get sense? Gold dust how na?” I chuckled and threw water at her. She dodged. “So why the margin? After all, both of them na Asians.” “Lantana. One is Eastern European while one is Asian.” I laughed and waddled further into the ocean. “Besides, one uses her house while the other pays rates and rents.” “Same of same ni. Asian oo, European oo, na the same colour.” “Oh, I forgot you failed Geography at WAEC and managed a pass in History. So why bother explaining it to you?” “Abeg free mẹ. European. Asian, no bi same oyiboo abi dem be black?” She giggled, like a schoolgirl who saw her boyfriend. “So that Egyptian guy now wey be African, you go call am Black sef?” I asked. “Those Arab-wannabes. Na African na–oyibo African.” “Lantana, I take God beg you, mbok. I no get your power. Let me enjoy my quiet time. At least this one is free” “But it won’t serve the same purpose na. That session would have done wonders to your body. Especially after these two days of hard training by Coach L. You can’t even lift your hands above your head from the pain.” “True. I looked forward to enjoying this experience. Especially after recovering from these last weeks. Also, the lymphatic drainage would have helped.” “Dis Obodo–oyinbo sef,” Lantana bristled “Kilode?” I stepped out of the water. “If this was Naija, they for no turn you back na. They would have made allowance for you.” “True. Pata pata, I go pay extra. And that one is even a total experience, not this mockery of a thing they call spa,” I begrudged. “Ah, babe, I miss Naija spa session.” “As in. From the moment you enter, you get the whole star treatment – sauna, steam, exfoliate, bathe before the massage begins. And sometimes pedicure join sef. All for how much na?” “Nne, don’t even go there. The money for that whole experience no still reach this £60 wey dem use for only massage. Let’s not go down to Egypt joo. Comparisons would only spoil this experience now.” “Which one?” She asked, spreading out her arms. “What did you think I was doing inside the water?” I side-eyed her. “Nothing na. Dem dey ask mamiwota wetin she dey do for her house?” She moved farther back as I stepped closer. “So now I don turn mamiwota because I come seaside?” I cackled. “Auntie, everybody know you and water na. It’s still a wonder how you take escape marine kingdom na your momsy head strong pass their own.” “See why I say you no get sense. So because the water is my happy place mean something now?” “No be only happy place. Water na your addiction.” “Na you get your mouth. I only came for cold water therapy, and I am done.” “Cold water therapy inside this cold and wind? You no see say e no normal abi you no get cold water for house?” “That Polish woman taught me the thing when I started going to her for alternative therapy. She said the cold water shock is cool for the system.” “Cold? Before, would it have been hot? A black person like you go dey behave like whitey. Carry cold water dey pour for body. Yet, una dey complain say boarding house wicked.” “Not same. That was forced. This is a choice.” I wore my crocs and started ambling off. “Whose choice? Yours or your body’s? You just carry the poor body fling inside shocking cold water, and you say choice.” “Lantana, I go see you for house. I no get ya power now.” The post BN Prose: A Beachside Conversation Amara Nnaji appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: FBI pins $6.3B Binance crypto heist on North Korean hackers
item.description: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers. In an alert published Saturday , the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets. Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized. According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace. The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds. The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange , the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making. Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals , which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity. The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill. That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets. Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach. TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024 . The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems. As we reported here on Friday , crypto exchange Bi
item.dc:creator: Carly Page
item.content:encoded: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers. In an alert published Saturday , the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets. Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized. According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace. The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds. The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange , the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making. Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals , which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity. The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill. That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets. Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach. TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024 . The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems. As we reported here on Friday , crypto exchange Bitget has now confirmed that the cyberattack where hackers drained $387.5 million worth of digital assets from the exchange’s wallets also has all the hallmarks of a North Korean operation. Its CEO did not go into too much detail, but did say that “IP behavioral patterns and on-chain signatures” suggest it was Kim’s cronies at work. This isn’t Binance's first expensive encounter with hackers, either. Back in 2022, attackers exploited its BNB blockchain bridge and made off with roughly $566 million in tokens. Four years later, the sums have grown considerably. Binance may have the reserves to make its customers whole, but the attackers responsible for the latest raid still have billions of dollars to launder. ®

item.title: WSL talking points: Kang could have a problem and how long can Slegers hang on?
item.description: Arsenal dropped points again despite dominating while Lauren James had to go off in Chelsea’s 6-0 win at Charlton London City Lionesses may have lost 2-1 to champions Manchester City, but their performances and league position have shown their European aspirations are far from unrealistic. Aided by Arsenal’s poor start, London City are third in the WSL table and were frustrated to end the day with a six-point gap to the top two after dominating in Bromley. “It’s doubly frustrating, because I think the result was not the one we deserve,” said their coach, Eder Maestre. “Manchester City are more mature. They are more used to it. When you have this consistency and you are very used to playing these kinds of games, maybe you have more experience.” Maestre’s team have a three-point lead over fourth-placed Tottenham and if they continue their upwards trajectory and qualify for the Champions League, Uefa will be forced to tackle the possible scenario of two Michele Kang-owned clubs, London City and OL Lyonnes, qualifying sooner than they perhaps anticipated.
